title: Write an ADR for every architecturally significant decision.
Keep ADRs in the repository next to the code as numbered Markdown files, for example `docs/decisions/0001-use-postgresql.md`.
Record the options you considered and why you rejected them, not just the option you chose.
Don't rewrite accepted decisions. Supersede them with a new ADR and link the two.
Say how compliance will be confirmed, for example with a design or code review, an architecture test such as ArchUnit, or a fitness function.
Decentralise decisions with an advice process.
Treat model inputs and outputs as untrusted.
Start with the simplest solution, such as a single model call with retrieval.
Build evaluations early and run them on every change to prompts, models or tools.
Use workflows (predefined code paths) for well-defined tasks, and agents only where the model must decide the steps itself.
Design tools specifically for agents, and put as much effort into the agent interface as you would into a human one: clear, distinct names, focused scope and actionable error messages.
Treat context as a finite resource and curate what goes into it.
Budget for the hidden technical debt of ML systems: data dependencies, feedback loops and glue code.
Don't be afraid to launch without machine learning.
Use a UI layer and a data layer, and add a domain layer only when logic is complex or reused.
Keep a single source of truth for each data type, and use unidirectional data flow: state flows down, events flow up.
Expose UI state from ViewModels as observable streams, and keep UI elements free of business logic.
Access data only through repositories in the data layer.
Use dependency injection (Hilt).
Follow the coroutine best practices: inject dispatchers, make suspend functions main-safe, and don't expose mutable state.
Build offline-first where possible, with the local database as the source of truth.
Modularise by feature and layer as the app and team grow.

Keep the current defaults in new code: standalone components, `OnPush` change detection and zoneless change detection. Don't set `standalone: false`, `ChangeDetectionStrategy.Eager` or `provideZoneChangeDetection()`.

Derive state with `computed()`, or with `linkedSignal()` when the user can also set it, and use `effect()` only to sync signals with APIs that aren't reactive, such as storage, logging, or a canvas or third-party UI library.

Declare inputs, outputs and queries with the signal-based functions, such as `input()`, `output()`, `model()` and `viewChild()`, and name outputs in camelCase, without an `on` prefix and without the name of a DOM event such as `click`.

Use the built-in control flow (`@if`, `@for` and `@switch`) instead of the deprecated `*ngIf`, `*ngFor` and `*ngSwitch`, and give every `@for` a `track` expression with a property that uniquely identifies the item, such as its ID.

Keep components focused on presentation, and move business logic, data access and state that several components share into services. Keep that state in private writable signals, and expose it as read-only signals, with `asReadonly()` or `computed()`, plus methods that change it.

Declare app-wide services with `@Service()`, or with `@Injectable({providedIn: 'root'})` before Angular 22, inject dependencies with `inject()`, and provide a service in a route's `providers` instead when only one feature uses it.
Read data that depends on signals with `httpResource()`, convert Observables that templates read with `toSignal()`, and send changes, such as `POST` and `PUT` requests, with `HttpClient` directly.
Lazy-load every route except the main landing pages with `loadComponent` or `loadChildren`, and wrap heavy components that aren't visible on the first render in `@defer` blocks.

In server-rendered apps, set a render mode for each route in the server routes: `RenderMode.Prerender` for pages that are the same for every user, `RenderMode.Server` for pages with user-specific data, and `RenderMode.Client` only where load performance and SEO matter less.
Give every route a `title`, and move focus to the main content after each navigation.
Never use route guards as access control: check authorization on the server for every request.
Never build Angular templates from user input: ship only templates that the CLI compiles ahead of time, and don't generate Angular templates with a server-side templating language.

Insert untrusted values through template bindings, so that Angular sanitizes them, never pass them to the `DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrust*()` methods, and don't write to the DOM through `ElementRef.nativeElement` or `document`.
Never put secrets, such as API keys, in the files in `src/environments/`: the build bundles them into the client, where anyone who loads the page can read them.

Send a Content Security Policy with a unique, unpredictable nonce for each response, and pass the nonce to Angular with the `ngCspNonce` attribute or the `CSP_NONCE` token. On static hosting that can't add a nonce, turn on `autoCsp` or avoid inline scripts, instead of hard-coding a nonce.
Run a major version that is still supported, update with `ng update` one major version at a time, and plan each yearly major update before your version's long-term support ends.

Keep strict template type checking on (`strictTemplates`, the default) together with TypeScript's `strict` (`TS-1`), and make the extended diagnostics fail the build by setting their `defaultCategory` to `error`.

Test components the way users use them, and let Angular schedule change detection: drive shared UI components through component harnesses, await `fixture.whenStable()` instead of calling `fixture.detectChanges()`, and answer HTTP requests with `HttpTestingController`, then call `verify()`.
Make operations safe to retry, using idempotency keys where the method isn't naturally idempotent.
Evolve APIs in backward-compatible ways.
Use HTTP methods and status codes as their specification defines them.
Design the API contract first and review it before implementing it.
Model HTTP APIs around resources and standard methods, not ad-hoc RPC verbs.
Paginate list endpoints from day one.
Return machine-readable errors in the Problem Details format.
With enough users, every observable behaviour will be depended on by someone, whether documented or not (Hyrum's law).
Verify compatibility between providers and consumers with consumer-driven contract tests.
For gRPC and Protocol Buffers, follow the official dos and don'ts on field numbering and evolution.

Keep Astro's default static output, and render a route on demand with `export const prerender = false` only when it needs request data, such as cookies or a session. Switch to `output: 'server'` only when most pages are rendered on demand.

Add a `client:*` directive only to framework components that must be interactive, and choose the lowest priority that works: `client:idle`, `client:visible` or `client:media` for most islands, and `client:load` only for visible UI that must be interactive at once.

Render personalized parts of an otherwise static or cached page as server islands with `server:defer` and fallback content, pass them only the props they need, and set a constant `ASTRO_KEY` from `astro create-key` for rolling or multi-region deployments and CDN-cached pages.
Manage sets of structured content in content collections with a schema, and prefer build-time collections: use live collections only when content must be fresh on every request.
Keep local images in `src/` and render them with `<Image />` or `<Picture />` from `astro:assets`, and list only trusted remote hosts in `image.domains` or `image.remotePatterns`.
Treat every action as a public endpoint: give it an `input` schema, and check authorization in its handler, not only in middleware or on the page that calls it.

Declare environment variables in the `env.schema` of the Astro config, give a variable `context: "client"` or the `PUBLIC_` prefix only if its value may be public, and read secrets with `access: "secret"` from `astro:env/server`.
Render every page that depends on the visitor, such as pages behind a login or with personalized content, on demand, and check authentication on each request in middleware or in the page.
Pass request data, such as the current user, from middleware to pages and endpoints in `context.locals`, and keep data that must last between requests in Astro sessions or a database.
Keep `security.checkOrigin` on, which is the default, and when a trusted proxy sets `X-Forwarded-Host`, list your hosts in `security.allowedDomains` instead of allowing all.

Turn on `security.csp`, which adds hashes for Astro's own scripts and styles to a CSP `<meta>` element on every page, add your other directives in its options, and don't add `'unsafe-inline'`. Test it with `astro build` and `astro preview`, because it doesn't work in the dev server.

Prefer the browser's native cross-document view transitions, and add `<ClientRouter />` only for features that need it. With it, run code that must run on every page in an `astro:page-load` listener, and give every page a `<title>`, which the router announces to screen readers after each navigation.
Type-check in CI with `astro check`, for example as `astro check && astro build`, and use the `strict` or `strictest` tsconfig template.
Test `.astro` components with Vitest through `getViteConfig()` and the Container API, and run end-to-end tests with Playwright against a production build served by `astro preview`.
In browser apps, keep tokens out of reach of JavaScript: use a server-side session in a cookie, or a Backend for Frontend (BFF) that holds the OAuth tokens.
Use the authorization code flow with PKCE for every OAuth client. Don't use the implicit grant, and never use the resource owner password credentials grant.
Use an established identity provider, or your framework's built-in authentication and session management, instead of writing your own.
Sign users in through an external identity provider with OpenID Connect, not plain OAuth, and identify each federated user by issuer and subject (`iss` and `sub`).
Set session cookies with `Secure`, `HttpOnly` and `SameSite=Strict` or `Lax`, and prefer the `__Host-` name prefix.
Issue a new session ID when a user signs in, re-authenticates or changes privilege level, and invalidate the old one.
Enforce idle and absolute session timeouts on the server, and invalidate the session on the server when the user logs out.
Make sessions revocable: end all of a user's sessions when the account is disabled, and offer to end the other sessions after a password or MFA change.
Ask for the current credentials again before sensitive changes, such as a new password or email address, and before sensitive transactions.
Store passwords only as salted hashes from a slow password-hashing function: Argon2id, scrypt, bcrypt or PBKDF2.
Follow NIST's password rules: require at least 15 characters for passwords used alone (8 with MFA), allow at least 64, and reject passwords on a blocklist of common and breached ones.
Offer multi-factor authentication to all users, and require it for administrators and other privileged accounts.
Offer a phishing-resistant authenticator, preferably passkeys. When a passkey counts as a second factor, require user verification and check its flag on the server.
Give the same response, in about the same time, whether the account doesn't exist, the password is wrong or the account is locked, and limit failed attempts per account.
Protect account recovery as strongly as sign-in: use random, single-use, short-lived reset tokens, answer the same whether or not the account exists, and notify the user after every recovery.
Encourage users to register more than one passkey or authenticator, or to keep single-use recovery codes, so that losing one device doesn't force a weaker recovery.
Give people access through IAM Identity Center federation and workloads through IAM roles, so that both use temporary credentials instead of IAM users with long-term access keys.
Use a multi-account structure with AWS Organizations, separating workloads and environments into their own accounts.
Design for Availability Zone failure, and understand AWS fault isolation boundaries.
Define AWS infrastructure with the CDK or CloudFormation, and follow the CDK best practices for structuring apps, constructs and stacks.
Review each workload against the Well-Architected Framework early in design and before go-live, and again after significant architecture changes.
Choose a disaster recovery strategy from your RTO and RPO: backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, or multi-site active/active.
Set organisation-wide guardrails with service control policies.
In Lambda functions, separate the handler from the core logic, and reuse the execution environment for clients and connections.
Tag resources consistently for ownership, cost allocation and automation.
Contain the blast radius of failures with cell-based or shuffle-sharded designs where scale demands it.
Deploy workloads into an Azure landing zone: put platform services such as management, connectivity and identity in their own subscriptions, and give each workload environment its own subscriptions.
Agree on a naming convention and a set of required tags, such as application, environment and cost center, before you deploy, and enforce the tags with Azure Policy.
Set guardrails with Azure Policy: prefer built-in policies and initiatives, assign them at the highest suitable scope, and roll out each new assignment in audit mode before you switch it to deny.
Keep the management group hierarchy flat, ideally three or four levels, and group subscriptions by workload type, such as corp and online, not by environment or org chart.
Authenticate workloads with managed identities, and pipelines and workloads outside Azure with workload identity federation, instead of client secrets, certificates or access keys.
Use one Key Vault per application, environment and region, authorize access with Azure RBAC rather than legacy access policies, and turn on purge protection.
Assign Azure RBAC roles to groups rather than users, at the narrowest scope, keep at most three subscription owners, and give administrators just-in-time access with Privileged Identity Management.
Reach PaaS data services, such as Storage, SQL Database and Key Vault, through private endpoints, and block public traffic with the service firewall or turn public network access off.
Deploy production workloads across availability zones in regions that have them, and prefer zone-redundant service configurations.
Define all Azure resources as code in Bicep or Terraform, deploy them from a pipeline, and build on Azure Verified Modules.

In Bicep, mark secret parameters and outputs with `@secure()`, don't give secure parameters default values, and read secrets from Key Vault with `getSecret()` or the `existing` keyword instead of passing them through outputs.
Route resource logs to a central Log Analytics workspace with diagnostic settings, deployed at scale with Azure Policy, and start with a single workspace.
Create a budget with actual and forecasted cost alerts for every subscription.
Assess each workload with the Azure Well-Architected Review, and act on Azure Advisor recommendations, which Advisor scores by pillar.
Give each service or module exclusive ownership of its data.
Evolve database schemas through small, versioned migrations kept in source control.
Keep data consistent across services with sagas, not distributed transactions.
Publish events atomically with state changes using a transactional outbox.
Choose the consistency level per use case and make eventual consistency visible in the design.
Choose storage technology per need, but count the operational cost of every extra datastore.
At organisational scale, treat analytical data as a product owned by domain teams (data mesh).
Set recovery point and recovery time objectives for each data store, back up to meet them with copies kept outside the primary system, and test restores regularly.
Assume every message can arrive more than once: acknowledge it only after processing it, and make consumers idempotent, for example by recording the IDs of processed messages.
Build a ubiquitous language with domain experts and use it everywhere: in conversations, documents and code.
Split large domains into bounded contexts, each with its own model, and make the relationships between them explicit.
Spend modelling effort on the core domain; buy or simplify generic subdomains.
Use aggregates as consistency boundaries.
Put behaviour next to the data it changes and avoid anemic domain models.
Model concepts that are defined by their attributes as immutable value objects.
Keep Electron's secure renderer defaults: context isolation, the sandbox and `webSecurity` on, and Node.js integration off. Call `app.enableSandbox()` so that no window can turn the sandbox off.

In Electron preload scripts, expose a narrow API with `contextBridge.exposeInMainWorld`: one function per IPC message, using `ipcRenderer.invoke` for requests. Never expose `ipcRenderer` or its `send`, `invoke` or `on` methods, and don't pass the IPC event object to callbacks in the page.
In Electron's main process, check the sender of every IPC message, for example the origin of `event.senderFrame`, and validate its arguments before acting on them.

Treat the arguments of every Tauri command as untrusted input: deserialize them into specific types, check their values in the command, and enforce your own scopes in the command itself. Keep secrets and as much business logic as you can in the Rust core.

Never block Electron's main process: use the asynchronous versions of Node.js APIs, avoid `ipcRenderer.sendSync` and `@electron/remote`, and move CPU-heavy, crash-prone or untrusted work to a worker thread or a utility process.

Give every window a Content Security Policy that allows only your own scripts, such as `script-src 'self'`: in Electron, send it as a header from `session.webRequest.onHeadersReceived`, or in a `<meta>` tag for pages that can't get headers; in Tauri, set `app.security.csp` in `tauri.conf.json`, because Tauri's CSP protection is off until you set it.

Grant each Tauri window only the permissions it needs: give windows with different privileges separate capabilities, add a window to several capabilities only if it needs all their permissions, declare your own commands with `AppManifest::commands` in `build.rs` so that a window can call them only when a capability allows it, and let only higher-privileged windows create windows.

Scope every Tauri plugin permission that reaches the system: allow file system access only to the base directories the app needs, such as `$APPDATA`, with deny scopes for sensitive paths, allow the shell plugin to run only named programs with argument validators, and allow the opener plugin only the URLs and paths it needs.

Limit where Electron windows can go: block navigation in a `will-navigate` handler unless a parsed URL matches the pages you expect, deny new windows in `setWindowOpenHandler` by default, and pass only checked, allowlisted URLs to `shell.openExternal`.

Serve Electron's local pages from a custom protocol with `protocol.handle` instead of `file://`, and flip the fuses you don't need when packaging, before code signing: turn off `RunAsNode`, `EnableNodeOptionsEnvironmentVariable`, `EnableNodeCliInspectArguments` and `GrantFileProtocolExtraPrivileges`, and turn on `EnableEmbeddedAsarIntegrityValidation` and `OnlyLoadAppFromAsar`.
Use Tauri's isolation pattern when the front end has many dependencies or loads third-party content, and keep the isolation application small, with few dependencies and build steps.

Never build API keys or other secrets into the app, and store users' credentials and tokens only in encrypted storage: in Electron, the asynchronous `safeStorage` API, which uses the operating system's cryptography, and in Tauri, for example, the Stronghold plugin.

Sign every release in the release pipeline: sign macOS apps with a Developer ID Application certificate and notarize them, and sign Windows executables and installers with one consistent identity, as `STEAM-16` describes.

Deliver updates only through a signed update mechanism over HTTPS: Electron's `autoUpdater`, for example through `update-electron-app`, in a signed app, or the Tauri updater with its signing key pair. Keep the update signing key in the CI secret store, and never set the Tauri updater's `dangerousInsecureTransportProtocol`.

Stay on an Electron major that the Electron team still supports, which is one of the latest three, on its latest minor release, and upgrade one major at a time. Update Tauri, the Rust compiler and Node.js just as promptly.

Run end-to-end tests against the built app, for example with WebdriverIO's Electron or Tauri service, or with Playwright's experimental Electron support, and mock the IPC layer in front-end unit tests, for example with Tauri's `mockIPC`.
Start with a system context diagram and a container diagram.
Store, version and review documentation alongside the code.
Give every diagram a title, a key or legend, and labelled, directed relationships.
Keep diagrams as text in the repository so they can be reviewed and diffed.
Use the C4 abstractions (person, software system, container, component) consistently, whatever the notation.
Don't mix tutorials, how-to guides, reference and explanation in one document.
Run the application as a non-root user: create a user in the Dockerfile and switch to it with `USER`.
Never pass secrets to a build through `ARG`, `ENV` or copied files. Use secret mounts or SSH mounts.
Pin base images to a tag plus digest, and let a bot such as Dependabot update both.
Use multi-stage builds so that the final image contains only what the application needs to run, on a small base image from a trusted source.
Rebuild images often, with `--pull` to fetch fresh base images, so that security fixes in the base image reach production.
Start the main process with the exec form, such as `ENTRYPOINT ["app"]`, so that it runs as PID 1 and receives `SIGTERM`.
Order Dockerfile instructions from least to most often changed: copy the dependency manifests and install dependencies before copying the source code.
Keep the build context small with a `.dockerignore` file.
Give each container one concern: run the web app, the database and the cache as separate containers.
Scan images for known vulnerabilities in CI, fail the build above an agreed severity, and keep scanning the images you have deployed.
Attach SBOM and provenance attestations to the images you publish, and sign them so that deployments can verify where an image came from.
Never mount the Docker socket into a container, and never expose the daemon over unauthenticated TCP.
Run containers with least privilege: never use `--privileged`, drop all capabilities and add back only those needed, set `no-new-privileges`, and use a read-only root file system where possible.
Give containers runtime secrets as Compose or orchestrator secrets, mounted as files, rather than as environment variables.
Make services wait for their dependencies to be ready, not only started: give the dependency a `healthcheck` and use `depends_on` with `condition: service_healthy`.

Keep one base `compose.yaml` and put environment-specific changes in extra files, such as `compose.override.yaml` for development and `compose.production.yaml` for production. In production, don't bind-mount application code.
Load secrets through configuration providers: user secrets (the Secret Manager) in development, and Azure Key Vault or another vault in production, never `appsettings.json` or source code.
Go async all the way and never block on async code with `.Result` or `.Wait()`.
Use the built-in DI container and follow its lifetime guidelines.
Add `AddStandardResilienceHandler` from `Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience` to outgoing `HttpClient`s.

When the domain has real business logic, structure the solution with Clean Architecture: an application core that defines interfaces, and infrastructure projects that implement them and that the core never references.
Register `AddProblemDetails` and `UseExceptionHandler`, so that errors are returned as ProblemDetails and exceptions are handled in one place.
Map separate liveness and readiness endpoints with `MapHealthChecks`, selecting the checks for each by tag.
Instrument with the OpenTelemetry .NET SDK, or with the .NET Aspire service defaults, which configure it for you.
Enable nullable reference types in all projects.
Test the HTTP pipeline with in-memory integration tests (`WebApplicationFactory`), and enforce layering with architecture tests.
Bind configuration to strongly typed classes with the options pattern.
Follow the EF Core performance guidance for queries and change tracking.

Start every Firestore database, Realtime Database and Storage bucket with rules that deny all access, and never deploy test-mode rules, `allow read, write: if true`, or rules that let any signed-in user (`request.auth != null`) reach all data.

Write the rules for each new collection or path together with the code that uses it, keep the rules and index definitions (`firestore.rules`, `storage.rules` and `firestore.indexes.json`) in the repository, and deploy them with the Firebase CLI instead of editing them in the console.

Unit-test the rules with `@firebase/rules-unit-testing` against the emulators, asserting with `assertSucceeds` and `assertFails` that allowed requests succeed and forbidden ones fail, and run the tests in CI with `firebase emulators:exec`.

Validate every client write in the rules: allow only known fields with `request.resource.data.keys().hasOnly()`, check their types, and use `diff().affectedKeys()` to stop clients from changing fields such as an owner ID, a role or a balance.
Keep fields that not every reader may see in a separate document, such as a private subcollection with its own rules, because rules allow or deny reads of whole documents.
If you use anonymous authentication, protect all non-public data with rules that require a permanent sign-in provider or a verified email address, because anyone can create an anonymous account.

Enforce App Check for every product that supports it, such as Firestore, Realtime Database, Cloud Storage, Authentication and callable functions, once its request metrics show that your current app versions send valid tokens.

Treat Firebase API keys and Remote Config values as public: restrict each API key to the APIs it needs, use a separate restricted key for any API that isn't a Firebase service, and never put a Gemini Developer API key, a service account key or another server credential in a client.

Harden Firebase Authentication before launch: disable the sign-in providers you don't use, enable email enumeration protection, tighten the quota of the sign-in endpoints, and allow only your own domains.

Use a separate Firebase project for each environment, such as development, staging and production, register debug and release builds in different projects, and don't put unrelated apps in one project.

Model Firestore data around the queries your screens run and what they cost: each document a query returns, each document a listener receives when it's added or changed, and each document a rule reads with `get()` or `exists()` is billed as a read.
Turn on point-in-time recovery and scheduled backups for production Firestore databases.
Give Cloud Functions their credentials through Secret Manager, with `defineSecret()` bound only to the functions that need each secret, not through `.env` files or `functions.config()`.

Make event-triggered functions idempotent, for example by using the event ID as an idempotency key, turn on retries only for transient errors, and test on the emulators that a function's writes can't trigger it again in a loop.

Set budget alerts on every project on the pay-as-you-go Blaze plan, add spend caps for the services that support them, such as Cloud Functions, and limit each function's maximum number of instances to what normal traffic needs.

Where users must consent to analytics or crash reporting, set the Google Analytics consent defaults in the app's configuration, update them with `setConsent()` when the user decides, and turn on Crashlytics opt-in reporting.
Separate the UI layer (views and view models) from the data layer (repositories and services), and add a domain layer of use cases only when needed.
Make repositories the source of truth for app data, with services that wrap external APIs.
Use unidirectional data flow and immutable data models.
Cover logic with unit tests, widgets with widget tests, and critical flows with integration tests.
Choose a state management approach that fits the app and the team, and use it consistently for app state. `setState` is fine for widget-local state.
Model user actions as commands, and model operation outcomes as `Result` values instead of throwing across layers.
Advance the simulation in fixed time steps, decoupled from the render rate, and interpolate between the last two simulated states when rendering.
Build game entities by composing components, not through deep inheritance hierarchies.
Define entity types and tuning values as data that designers can change without recompiling, not as one subclass per type.
Adopt an entity component system (ECS) deliberately, when you need very large numbers of entities, and prefer an established framework to writing your own.
In competitive multiplayer games, make the server authoritative: clients send inputs, and the server runs the simulation and sends back the results.
Hide latency with client-side prediction and server reconciliation.
Render other players slightly in the past, interpolating between buffered server updates, instead of snapping to each update as it arrives.
For hit detection in fast-paced shooters, use lag compensation: the server rewinds the world to the moment the shooter saw it and checks the hit there.
Choose deterministic lockstep, which sends only inputs, only if the simulation is bit-for-bit deterministic on every platform you ship to. Otherwise, synchronise state.
Version the save-data schema from the first release, and migrate older saves to the current version when loading them.
Keep the last good save until the new one is completely written, and store an integrity check so that a corrupt or partial save falls back to the previous one.
Set a frame-time budget for each target platform (33.3 ms at 30 fps, 16.7 ms at 60 fps), and measure against it with a profiler on the target hardware, before and after each optimisation.
Pool objects that are created and destroyed often, such as projectiles and particles, instead of allocating and freeing each one.
Rearrange data for cache locality only where profiling shows that cache misses cost time.
Pick version control that handles large binary assets before the project grows: Git with Git LFS, or a system built for binaries such as Perforce.

Lock binary assets that can't be merged, such as levels, textures, models and audio, before editing them: mark their types `lockable` in `.gitattributes` with Git LFS, or check them out exclusively in Perforce.
Plan accessibility at the design stage: review the Game Accessibility Guidelines before work starts, choose the ones that apply, and schedule early the ones that are costly to add later.
Address the four most common complaints first: control remapping, text size, colour blindness and subtitle presentation.
Don't convey essential information by colour alone or by sound alone, and give effects, speech and music separate volume controls.
Use the Xbox Accessibility Guidelines as a test checklist for your game's accessibility features.
Don't rely on the order in which instances run the same event, or on the order in which a room creates its instances.
Declare every instance variable in the Create event, or as an Object Variable, and use `var` for values that only one event needs.
Refer to a particular instance through its instance ID, and use the object name only in code meant for all its instances.

Put behaviour that a family of objects shares in a parent object that is never placed in a room itself, and call `event_inherited()` in a child's event when the parent's code for that event should also run.

Keep game-wide state in a few known places: declare every global variable in one script function or one controller object at the start of the game, always with the `global.` prefix, and define all macros in a dedicated script asset.
Make an object persistent only if its instance must outlive the room, such as a game manager or the player, and create that instance exactly once.
Define global functions in script assets with `function name() {}`, and functions inside objects and constructors as method variables, `name = function() {}`, so that children can override them.

Use constructors and structs, not object instances, for data and logic that need no events, drawing or collisions, such as stats, inventories or states, and declare their methods `static` so that all structs from a constructor share one copy.

Don't depend on the order in which function arguments or parts of an expression are evaluated: call functions with side effects, such as `buffer_read`, in separate statements, and use brackets in expressions.
Document script functions and constructors with JSDoc comments that give the types of `@param` and `@return`, and let Feather check types.
Use the asynchronous versions of slow operations, such as HTTP requests, file loading and adding sprites, and in the Async event check that `async_load[? "id"]` matches the request ID you stored.

Model objects with distinct modes, such as enemies, the player or menu buttons, as finite state machines: one state variable, states named by an enum, and the state code that a family shares in its parent object.
Build menus and the HUD in UI layers, with Flex Panels so that the layout adapts to the display, and place the objects that handle their input in those layers.

Choose the multiplayer approach before building gameplay: Rollback Multiplayer plays online only on the GX.games target and shares only input, so every client must run the same logic, and for other platforms use the Photon extension or your own server with the networking functions.

Keep texture swaps and vertex batches low: draw instances that need the same blend mode or shader together, from one controller object or through layer begin and end scripts, instead of letting each instance set and reset the state.

Undo every GPU state change on every code path before the code that made it ends: `shader_reset()` after `shader_set()`, `surface_reset_target()` after `surface_set_target()`, and the blend mode and other `gpu_set_*` settings back to their defaults.

Treat every surface except the application surface as volatile: check `surface_exists()` before each use and re-create the surface if it's gone, create and draw to surfaces in Draw events, keep them no larger than the view, and free them with `surface_free()`.

Fit the game to each display with a camera and viewport, and resize the application surface to match, instead of relying on the Full Scale option, which stretches the image and ignores the aspect ratio. For pixel art, also turn off *Interpolate colours between pixels*, which is on by default, in each platform's Game Options.

Make every image fit on the smallest texture page of any platform you ship to, check the pages with the Preview button in each platform's Game Options, and turn on mipmaps for texture groups that the camera zooms in and out on or that a 3D game uses.

Write shaders in GLSL ES, the only shader language that works on every target, follow its specification strictly, and check `shader_is_compiled()` at start-up before you use any shader that isn't simple GLSL ES.
Profile the game on every target device, during development and before and after each optimisation, with the Debugger's Profiler and the Debug Overlay.

Test and debug on the VM, but build the release of a CPU-heavy game with YYC on the platforms that offer it, measure its performance in that build, and clear the compiler cache before every final build.

Destroy everything you create at run time that has a destroy function, such as data structures, surfaces and buffers, usually in the Clean Up event, and use arrays and structs rather than DS lists and maps.

Assign sprites, tile sets and fonts to texture groups by where they're used, such as one group per level and one for the menus, and keep groups that only some rooms need out of memory: make them dynamic, load them with `texturegroup_load()` before they're needed, and unload them afterwards.
Choose each sound's compression by its length and use, and put sounds that only some rooms need in audio groups that you load with `audio_group_load()`.
Build static scenery from tile layers rather than instances with sprites, and check collisions against the tile map where the level fits a grid.

If you deactivate instances outside the view, do it every few steps or when the camera moves, never every step or in a Draw event, and reactivate persistent instances at least one step before the room changes.

Follow the manual's advice against losing saves: write each save to a new file, check it, then replace the old one, validate a save, for example with a checksum, before loading it, and keep files open only briefly.
Keep every project in source control from the first day, and keep the `.gitignore` and `.gitattributes` files that GameMaker adds to new and imported projects.

Save and close the project in GameMaker before you pull, merge, switch branches or revert with an external Git client, and if GameMaker reports changed files while the project is open, choose Reload, not Save.
Name every asset with a prefix for its type, such as `spr_`, `obj_`, `snd_` and `ts_`, agree on one way to group the Asset Browser, by asset type or by level, and set matching Feather naming rules.
Develop on the LTS release, use one IDE and runtime version across the team and the build machines, and upgrade everyone together, after committing, when you choose to.

Compile every pull request in CI, with `gm-cli compile` or with Igor on your own build machine, and pin both the `gm-cli` version and the runtime version, which `gm-options.json` records in its `toolchain` field.
Use configurations for what differs between builds of the same game, such as platforms, stores or a demo, and select the configuration in every build.
Share scripts and assets that several projects use as a Local Asset Package (`.yymps`) with a Package ID and version number, and update a project by importing the new version.

Test the logic in script functions and constructors, and the behaviour of objects over several frames, with a GML testing library such as GMTL, and run the tests every time you run the game in development.
Smoke-test every target build automatically with Igor's test command.
If you use Rollback Multiplayer, test every change in Sync Test, on Windows, macOS or GX.games, before you test online.

Drive each game server through the hosting platform's lifecycle with its server SDK: report ready only when it can accept players, keep its health checks passing, mark it allocated when a match starts, and end the process when the match is over.

Ship the server as its own headless build without rendering, audio or client-only assets: Unity's Dedicated Server build target, an Unreal `Server` target, or a Godot export preset in *Export as dedicated server* mode.
Choose the lowest tick rate that gives an acceptable player experience, and keep each tick within its time budget, with no database or HTTP calls inside it.
Don't let a scale-down or node maintenance end a running match.
Scale each fleet with a buffer of ready servers: start with a generous buffer and a maximum well above the expected peak, and lower the buffer later from real usage.
Handle the shutdowns you can't prevent: when the platform signals termination, stop accepting players, save the match state, disconnect players cleanly and exit before the deadline.
Run game servers in more than one region, and in more than one cluster or fleet per region, and allocate across them, so that one failed cluster doesn't stop matches from starting.
Let a backend service that authenticates players request matches and game servers for them, and take skill ratings and other matching attributes from server-side data, not from the client.

Place each match in the region with the lowest measured latency for its players: have clients time UDP round trips to each region, send the results with the matchmaking request, cap the latency you accept, and relax the limits step by step while players wait.
Roll out new server builds without ending running matches: start the new version next to the old one, send new matches to it, and let the old servers exit when their matches end.
Version the network protocol, check the version when a client connects, and reject clients that don't match; send players only to servers running a build compatible with their client.

Before launch, replace every default credential and close every administration port: change Nakama's `socket.server_key`, `session.encryption_key`, `runtime.http_key` and console password, and close RDP (3389) and SSH (22) on live fleets.
Admit to a match only the players the matchmaker placed in it: the client presents its player session or ticket, and the server validates it before accepting the connection.
Keep player inventories, currencies, progression and scores in data that only server code can write.
Rate-limit each player's actions and traffic, and protect game servers from DDoS attacks, for example with a relay that hides their IP addresses.

Record tick time and achieved tick rate for every game server, along with players, active sessions and crashed or abnormally terminated sessions, and alert on severe problems such as ticks that overrun their budget.
Use one organization resource, with folders for environments or other policy boundaries, and a separate project for each workload in each environment.
Label projects and resources consistently, for example with application, environment, cost center and owner, and set the labels from infrastructure as code.
Don't grant basic roles, such as Owner, Editor and Viewer, in production. Grant predefined or custom roles to groups, at the smallest scope that works.

Don't use service account keys: attach service accounts to workloads that run on Google Cloud, use Workload Identity Federation for CI pipelines and workloads elsewhere, and block key creation with an organization policy.

Give each application its own single-purpose service account instead of a default service account, and grant users the Service Account User and Token Creator roles on individual service accounts, not on projects or folders.
Enforce the Google Cloud security baseline constraints in every organization, including organizations created before 3 May 2024, which may not have them.

Add further Organization Policy constraints at the organization or folder level, starting from the enterprise foundations blueprint's set, and test each new policy in dry-run mode before you enforce it.
Keep secrets in Secret Manager, grant access per secret when one project holds secrets for many services, and reference secret versions by number instead of `latest`.
Put projects that hold sensitive data, for example in Cloud Storage or BigQuery, inside VPC Service Controls perimeters in addition to IAM, and run each new perimeter in dry-run mode first.
Deploy production workloads across multiple zones, and across regions where your availability or recovery targets require it.
Manage the organization's foundation and all workloads as code with Terraform, applied from a pipeline that validates changes against your policies, as the enterprise foundations blueprint does.
Route audit logs from the whole organization to a central project with an aggregated sink, and turn on Data Access audit logs for services that handle sensitive data.
Create Cloud Billing budgets with alert thresholds for each billing account or project, and send the alerts to the owners or to Pub/Sub for automated responses.
Choose the graphics API or engine render pipeline, and the oldest hardware you will support, at the start of the project, and record the choice and the options you rejected in an ADR.

Break each platform's frame-time budget (`GAMEDEV-12`) down into GPU budgets for each device tier: GPU time per frame, shader cycles, triangle counts, and memory for textures, meshes and render targets.

Before optimising, find out whether the frame is CPU-bound or GPU-bound, and which GPU stage limits it. Measure frame times in milliseconds with vsync off, not frames per second, and measure again after each change, because the bottleneck moves.

Inspect GPU frames with a frame debugger and GPU profiler for each target API: RenderDoc for Vulkan, Direct3D and OpenGL ES, PIX for Direct3D 12, the Metal debugger in Xcode for Apple GPUs, and Android GPU Inspector or the GPU vendor's profiler on Android.

Don't compile shaders or create pipeline state objects during gameplay. Create them while loading or on background threads, and keep them between runs in a pipeline cache (`VkPipelineCache`, a Direct3D 12 pipeline library) or as precompiled binaries where the platform allows, such as Metal binary archives.

Keep the number of shader variants small and known: count them in every build, strip those no material uses, and use dynamic branching, specialization constants or an ubershader for features that don't need a variant of their own.
Compile every shader for every target API offline, in CI, and validate the output, so that a shader that fails on one platform breaks the build rather than the game.

Run development and automated test builds with the graphics API's validation turned on, such as the Vulkan validation layers with Best Practices, the Direct3D 12 debug layer or Metal API Validation, and fix what they report.

Use 16-bit precision (`mediump` or explicit 16-bit types) wherever it is accurate enough, especially in fragment shaders on mobile GPUs, and check the results on a mobile GPU, because desktop GPUs usually ignore `mediump`.
Cut draw calls and state changes: cull objects outside the view on the CPU, batch or instance objects that share a material, and sort draws by pipeline state.

Draw opaque geometry front to back and transparent geometry back to front, and avoid `discard` and depth writes in fragment shaders where you can, so that early depth testing removes hidden fragments before they are shaded.

On tile-based GPUs, which include most mobile GPUs and Apple silicon, choose every attachment's load and store action deliberately: clear or don't-care on load unless you need the previous contents, and don't-care on store for attachments you don't read later, such as depth and multisampled color, which can then be transient or memoryless.

Ship textures in GPU-compressed formats, with mipmaps for anything seen in 3D: ASTC, with ETC2 as the fallback, on mobile, BC formats on desktop, and on the web a format each device supports, for example by transcoding Basis Universal at load time.
Give meshes that move towards and away from the camera levels of detail, with about half the triangles at each level, so that distant objects don't cost more than they show.
Feature-detect WebGPU and keep a WebGL 2 fallback, or use an engine that has one.
Handle a lost GPU context: listen for `webglcontextlost` and `webglcontextrestored` in WebGL, and watch `GPUDevice.lost` in WebGPU, and be able to recreate every GPU resource.
Set the `GITHUB_TOKEN` to read-only at the top of each workflow, and grant write permissions only to the jobs that need them.
Pin third-party actions and reusable workflows to a full-length commit SHA, or lock them with a workflow dependency lockfile.
Never expand untrusted input, such as `${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}`, directly in a `run:` script. Pass it through an intermediate environment variable.
Use `pull_request` rather than `pull_request_target` unless fork pull requests need secrets or write access, and never execute pull request code in a `pull_request_target` or `workflow_run` workflow.
Authenticate to cloud providers with OpenID Connect instead of long-lived cloud secrets, and restrict the trust policy to specific repositories, branches or environments.
Avoid self-hosted runners in public repositories. Where you use them, prefer ephemeral just-in-time runners.
Enable Dependabot version updates for the `github-actions` ecosystem.
Treat restored caches as untrusted input: never cache secrets, and write caches only from workflows with trusted triggers.
Require approval from designated code owners for changes to `.github/workflows`.
Pass secrets to reusable workflows by name instead of with `secrets: inherit`.
Deploy through environments with protection rules: required reviewers, allowed deployment branches, and secrets scoped to the environment.
Share CI logic through reusable workflows (whole jobs) and composite actions (steps) instead of copying YAML between workflows and repositories.
Use concurrency groups to cancel superseded runs on the same branch and to stop deployments to the same environment from running at once.
Pin every `include` and CI/CD component to a commit SHA or to a protected tag, pin job images by digest, and let a bot such as Renovate propose updates.
Keep secrets in an external secrets manager. If a secret must be a CI/CD variable, make it masked and hidden, and protected so that only pipelines for protected branches and tags receive it.
Authenticate to cloud providers and secret managers with ID tokens (`id_tokens`) instead of stored credentials, and restrict the trust policy to specific projects and protected branches or tags.
Run a pipeline in the parent project for a merge request from a fork only after reviewing its changes, including changes to `.gitlab-ci.yml`.

Don't use the shell executor or privileged Docker containers on runners that run jobs from several projects or untrusted users. Run privileged jobs only on isolated, ephemeral machines, and let runners that hold secrets or run privileged jobs take jobs from protected branches only.
Keep the CI/CD job token allowlist enabled, and add only the groups and projects that need cross-project access.
Pass parameters to pipelines as typed CI/CD inputs, and set the minimum role to use pipeline variables to `no_one_allowed` or Maintainer.
Never commit `CI_DEBUG_TRACE` to CI configuration, and turn on debug logging only temporarily, while only team members can view job logs.

Keep separate caches for protected and unprotected branches, which is the default, and don't set `cache:unprotect`. Pass build outputs between jobs as artifacts, and use the cache only for dependencies such as downloaded packages.
Require Code Owner approval for changes to `.gitlab-ci.yml` and other CI configuration on protected branches.

Use `rules` instead of the deprecated `only` and `except`, and don't mix them in one pipeline. Add `workflow:rules` that choose between branch and merge request pipelines, so that a push to a branch with an open merge request doesn't start two pipelines.

Run merge request pipelines, and enable merged results pipelines so that each merge request is tested combined with the latest target branch. Add merge trains when many merge requests are ready to merge at the same time.
Declare job dependencies with `needs`, so that each job starts as soon as the jobs it depends on finish, and give jobs that depend on nothing, such as linters, `needs: []`.
Share CI configuration as versioned CI/CD components with inputs instead of copying YAML between projects.
Deploy to production only through a protected environment: limit who can deploy, require deployment approvals, and scope production variables to that environment.
Give each deployment job a `resource_group`, so that only one deployment to an environment runs at a time, and turn on "Prevent outdated deployment jobs".

Lay out a service as "Organizing a Go module" describes for a server project: each command in `cmd/<name>/`, the packages that implement them under `internal/`, and each package named for what it provides, not `util`, `common` or `helper`.

Define interfaces in the package that uses them, keep them small, and return concrete types; don't add an interface before a consumer needs it, and don't export one from the implementing package only so that it can be mocked.
Check every error, then either handle it or return it with added context, not both: don't discard errors with `_`, and don't log an error that you return.

Return an `error` for every failure a caller can expect, such as invalid input, failed I/O or bad configuration, and panic only for bugs that tests and reviews should catch, such as API misuse or a broken invariant. In a server, recover at the top of each goroutine that serves one connection, job or match.

Pass the request's `context.Context` along the whole call chain, from the incoming request to every outgoing call, as the first parameter, named `ctx`; never store it in a struct, and use the context-aware APIs, such as `QueryContext` and `http.NewRequestWithContext`.

Make it obvious when each goroutine you start will end: give it a context to stop on, and wait for it with a `sync.WaitGroup` or an `errgroup.Group` from `golang.org/x/sync` before the code that started it returns or shuts down.

Never share a variable between goroutines without synchronization: hand data over on channels, or guard shared state, such as a cache, with a `sync.Mutex`, and run the tests with the race detector (`go test -race`) in CI.

Create every `http.Server` yourself and set its timeouts: always `ReadHeaderTimeout` and `IdleTimeout`, and `ReadTimeout` and `WriteTimeout` too unless handlers set their own deadlines. Don't serve with `http.ListenAndServe` or `http.Serve`, which can't set timeouts.

Shut down on `SIGTERM`: derive the root context from `signal.NotifyContext(ctx, os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM)`, and when it's done, call `Server.Shutdown` with a deadline shorter than the platform's grace period.

Log with `log/slog`: in a service, set a JSON handler on stdout as the default logger, with `slog.SetDefault(slog.New(slog.NewJSONHandler(os.Stdout, nil)))`, call the `...Context` logging methods so that handlers can add trace context, and give types that hold secrets a `LogValue` method that redacts them.
Commit `go.mod` and `go.sum`, change dependencies only with `go get` or `go mod tidy` in a reviewed change, and fail CI when `go mod tidy -diff` reports a difference.

Build with a supported Go release, one of the two newest major versions, at its latest minor version, and run `govulncheck` on every change in CI and regularly on the code or binaries you have deployed.

Never build SQL statements or HTML by formatting or concatenating strings with values: pass values to SQL as arguments for placeholders (`?` or `$1`), and render HTML with `html/template`, not `text/template`.

Open one `sql.DB` for each database when the program starts and share it, because it is a connection pool that is safe for concurrent use, and close every `sql.Rows` with `defer rows.Close()` and check `rows.Err()`.
In CI, fail the build on unformatted code (`gofmt -l`), on any `go vet ./...` finding and on linter findings, for example from Staticcheck or golangci-lint.

Fuzz the code that parses untrusted input, such as request decoders and network protocol handlers, with `go test -fuzz`, and test code with timers, timeouts or background goroutines inside `synctest.Test` instead of waiting in real time.
Commit the `.import` files next to your assets and the `.uid` files next to your scripts and shaders, and ignore the `.godot/` folder.
Use snake_case for file and folder names (C# scripts excepted), and keep third-party code in `addons/`.
Design scenes to work on their own: keep what a scene needs inside it, and let the parent supply any outside dependency.
Let parents call methods on and set properties of their children, and let children report what happened through signals.
Use autoloads only for broad-scoped systems that manage their own data, such as a quest or dialogue system.
Reference other nodes through `@export` properties or scene-unique names (`%Name`), not long hard-coded node paths.
Make game-specific concepts scenes, and use named script classes for reusable tools shared across projects.
Use `RefCounted` or `Resource` classes instead of nodes for data and logic that don't need to be in the scene tree.
Use static typing throughout, and set the `untyped_declaration` warning to Error so that untyped declarations stop a script from compiling.
Follow the GDScript style guide, including its code order.
Move objects and run game logic in `_physics_process`, and turn on physics interpolation so that motion stays smooth at any frame rate.
Model designer-edited game data as custom Resource classes saved as `.tres` files.
Write saves and settings to `user://`, and don't decode objects (`allow_objects`) from files that players can edit or share.
Write automated tests with GUT or gdUnit4, and run them headless in CI on every change.

Localize with Godot's translation system: add CSV or gettext PO translations under *Project Settings > Localization*, look up text with `tr()` and `tr_n()` or a Control's automatic translation, fill named placeholders with `String.format()`, and switch languages with `TranslationServer.set_locale()`.

Choose the renderer for the platforms and oldest hardware you ship to: Forward+ for desktop games that need advanced rendering features, Mobile for mobile devices and standalone XR, and Compatibility for the web, older devices or the widest hardware support.

In Forward+ and Mobile, let pipeline precompilation see everything during loading: show a simple scene that uses every rendering feature the game needs, such as MSAA, reflection probes or VoxelGI, before loading most assets, and instance effects that scripts add during play once as hidden nodes.
Reuse materials, and where you can't, reuse shaders: share one material across objects and give each object its own values through per-instance uniforms (`instance uniform`), not a unique material.
Draw thousands of identical objects, such as grass, flocks or particles, with a MultiMesh, and split it into several MultiMeshes by area, because Godot culls a MultiMesh only as a whole.

Keep the mesh LODs that Godot generates on import, and add visibility ranges (HLOD) where a group of objects should turn into one simpler mesh or an impostor in the distance, or where distant effects should disappear.

Choose the scripting languages early: GDScript suits most game code, C# suits teams that already know it, as long as you don't ship to the web, and C++ through GDExtension suits performance-critical algorithms.

Read player input through actions defined in the Input Map, not specific keys or buttons, and handle gameplay input events in `_unhandled_input()` rather than `_input()`, so that UI controls receive them first.

Set the base window size, stretch mode and stretch aspect at the start, following the docs' recommended settings for your kind of game, and lay out UI with anchors and Container nodes so that it adapts to every resolution and aspect ratio.

In multiplayer games, replicate spawned scenes with `MultiplayerSpawner` and properties with `MultiplayerSynchronizer`, keep the server the multiplayer authority over gameplay state, and give each player authority only over a child node that sends their input.

Don't change the active scene tree from another thread: build or load nodes outside the tree in the worker thread and add them on the main thread with `call_deferred()`, don't load the same resource from several threads at once, and protect data that threads share with a `Mutex`.

Profile on every target platform during development, not only in the editor: run a debug export with *Deploy with Remote Debug*, and use the debugger's Profiler for script time, the Visual Profiler for CPU and GPU rendering time, and the Monitors for memory and object counts.

Preload only what a script always needs, and load levels and other large or optional content in the background with `ResourceLoader.load_threaded_request()`, behind a loading screen, because `load()` blocks the thread until the resource has loaded.
Free nodes you no longer need with `queue_free()`: unlike `RefCounted` objects such as Resources, nodes aren't freed automatically, and `remove_child()` only takes a node out of the tree.

Import 3D textures as VRAM Compressed with mipmaps, which *Detect 3D* sets automatically, and 2D textures, especially pixel art, as Lossless; if the project needs other settings, change the defaults project-wide in *Project Settings > Import Defaults*.

Change imported 3D models in the modelling tool where you can, then in the import settings, and make any other change in an inherited scene, because Godot re-imports the whole scene whenever the source file changes.
Save scenes and resources in the text formats, `.tscn` and `.tres`, rather than the binary `.scn` and `.res`, so that they stay readable and easy to manage in version control.

If you store large assets in Git LFS (`GAMEDEV-15`), set it up before the first commit, starting from the example `.gitattributes` in Godot's version control documentation, which also tracks Godot's binary formats such as `.scn`, `.res`, `.mesh` and `.lmbake`.
Keep scripts and assets close to the scenes that use them, and move, rename or delete files only in Godot's FileSystem dock, so that references to them don't break.
Install third-party addons from the Asset Library or a tagged stable release, not from a repository's latest commit, and keep each one in its own `addons/<name>/` folder.
Commit `export_presets.cfg`, keep signing keys, passwords and encryption keys out of the repository, and automate release builds with `--export-release`.

Put platform- and build-specific project settings in feature-tag overrides, such as `.mobile`, `.web`, `.debug` or a custom tag set in an export preset, and read those settings with `ProjectSettings.get_setting_with_override()`.

Unit-test game logic in isolation, in `RefCounted` classes and other scripts that you can create with `new()`, and test whole scenes in integration tests with gdUnit4's Scene Runner or GUT's `simulate()` and input sender, for behaviour that spans frames or depends on input.
Let the code under test receive its dependencies, as `GODOT-3` describes for scenes, so that tests can replace them with GUT doubles and stubs or gdUnit4 mocks and spies.

Keep tests and the test framework out of release exports: put tests in their own folder, such as `res://test/`, and add it and the framework's addon folder (`addons/gut/*` or `addons/gdunit4/*`) to the exclude filter of every export preset.

Evolve the schema without versions: add fields and types, mark what you plan to remove with `@deprecated(reason: …)` naming the replacement, and remove it only after usage tracking shows that clients have migrated, or the announced deadline has passed.
Change data only in mutations: keep query fields free of side effects, and don't execute a mutation sent with `GET`.
Design the schema around the business domain and the way clients use the data, not around the database tables behind it.
Paginate every list field that can grow, with cursor-based connections that follow the Relay connection specification, and cap the page size.
Choose nullability field by field: keep a field nullable if it can fail or be denied on its own, make it non-null only where clients need the guarantee, and return lists as `[Item!]!`.
Return expected business errors, such as failed validation or a broken business rule, as typed results in the mutation's payload type, and keep the top-level `errors` array for unexpected failures.
Check authorization in the business logic layer that resolvers call, for every object and field a request reaches, including lookups by ID such as `node(id:)` and connection edges.

Limit what one request can cost: reject operations above a maximum depth, number of aliases and root fields, and number of operations in a batch, and stop execution after a timeout. For public APIs, also consider query cost analysis and rate limits based on cost.
If only your own clients call the API, execute only trusted documents in production: operations registered at build time and sent by ID.
Mask unexpected errors in production, and turn off stack traces and debug output.

Refuse requests that a browser can send cross-site without a CORS preflight, such as form-encoded or multipart bodies and `GET` requests without a custom header, to prevent cross-site request forgery.
Turn off introspection and GraphiQL in production for APIs that only your own clients use, and don't count on it as protection.
Batch and cache data loading within each request, with DataLoader or an equivalent, so that resolving a list doesn't call the backend once per item (the N+1 problem).
Start with one GraphQL service, and adopt federation only when several teams need to own and deploy parts of the graph independently.
Run code that queries a regional database or API in the same region as that backend, and keep edge execution for work that doesn't need it, such as redirects, rewrites, headers and geolocation.
Start new projects on each platform's recommended compute: the Node.js runtime on Vercel, and Workers with static assets on Cloudflare.
Keep each request well within the platform's duration, CPU, memory and payload limits, and move long or retryable work to background functions, queues or workflows.
Keep request and user data out of module-level variables and the local file system, and keep durable state in managed storage, such as a database, key-value store or blob store.

Connect to relational databases through connection pooling built for the platform: Hyperdrive on Cloudflare Workers, and on Vercel a pool created once per instance and registered with `attachDatabasePool`.

Set CDN caching deliberately on function responses: a shared-cache lifetime with `s-maxage` or `CDN-Cache-Control`, `stale-while-revalidate` where slightly stale content is acceptable, and `private` or `no-store` on per-user responses.
Tag cached responses with cache tags, and purge or invalidate them by tag when the underlying content changes.

Store credentials only as the platform's secret variables: Vercel Secret environment variables, Netlify variables marked as containing secret values, and Cloudflare secrets. Never put them in plain variables or in `vercel.json`, `netlify.toml` or Wrangler files.
Give production its own secrets and data stores, and don't let preview or development deployments use them.

Keep platform configuration in files in the repository, such as `vercel.json`, `netlify.toml` or the Wrangler configuration, and treat them as the source of truth instead of changing settings in the dashboard.

Keep preview deployments private: check that Vercel Deployment Protection or Netlify's private previews cover them, and put Cloudflare Access in front of Workers previews and Pages preview deployments, which are public by default.
Recover from a bad release by rolling back to the previous production deployment, and keep data and schema changes backward compatible so that the previous version still works.
Send logs and traces to an external observability service with a log drain or OpenTelemetry export, because the platforms keep runtime logs only for hours or days.
Keep every user-visible string, including error messages and console output, in resource files outside the code, so that it can be translated without changing the code, from the first release.
Never build a sentence by joining strings or fragments in code: put each complete message in one string, with named placeholders that translators can move.
Choose plural and gender forms with a message format that applies each language's CLDR plural rules, such as ICU MessageFormat, instead of testing `count == 1` in code.

Give translators context: a comment on every short or ambiguous string and on every placeholder that says where the text appears and what the placeholder will contain, plus screenshots or a test build where you can.
Write source text that is easy to translate: full sentences, plain words and consistent terms, without slang, jargon or cultural references, and proofread it before it goes to translators.
Use Unicode, encoded as UTF-8, wherever text is stored or exchanged: source and resource files, databases, files, APIs and protocols.

Format and parse dates, times, numbers, currencies and units, and sort text, with locale-aware APIs that use CLDR data, such as ICU, JavaScript `Intl` or your platform's globalization API, never with hand-written patterns or rules.
Store and exchange points in time as UTC timestamps, and convert them to the user's time zone only for display. For future and recurring events, such as meetings, also store the IANA time zone ID.

Treat the user-interface language, the regional formats and the user's country or region as separate settings: start from the operating system's or browser's preferences, let users change each one in the app, and be wary of guessing the language from the user's location or IP address.

Design layouts that adapt to the length and height of the text: let text wrap and controls grow, avoid fixed-width containers and text fitted tightly into graphics, and expect short strings to become two to three times as long as in English.
Lay out the user interface with start and end instead of left and right, so that it mirrors for right-to-left languages such as Arabic and Hebrew.
Use fonts that contain the glyphs of every script you ship, set fallback fonts for other scripts, and keep font names out of translatable strings.
Keep text out of images, textures and videos: draw it at run time from string resources, or use images without text.

Test with pseudo-localization from early in development: an automatic fake translation that accents each string, makes it about 40% longer and puts markers around it, plus a pseudo locale for formats.

Localize continuously: send new and changed strings to translation as soon as they're written, through an automated connection between the repository and the translation system, in a standard exchange format such as XLIFF.

Make each shared model an `@Observable` class, create it with `@State private var` in the view or `App` that owns it, and pass it down as a plain property, with `@Bindable` where a subview needs bindings, or through `.environment(_:)`.

Keep data and the logic that changes it in model types, not in views, and use `@State` only for state that a view owns: declare it `private` in the highest view that needs it, and pass the value or a binding to subviews.

Build every target in the Swift 6 language mode, which prevents data races at compile time. Migrate older modules one at a time, for example by setting Strict Concurrency Checking to Complete in the Swift 5 mode first and fixing the warnings.

Keep UI code and UI state on the main actor, and add concurrency only where you need it: set Default Actor Isolation to `MainActor` for app targets, run heavy work off the main actor with `@concurrent` functions, and keep other mutable state that tasks share in actors.

Prefer structured concurrency, `async let`, task groups and SwiftUI's `.task` modifier, to unstructured `Task { }`. When you do create a `Task`, keep its handle and cancel it when its work is no longer needed.

Store tokens, passwords and keys in the Keychain, with the most restrictive accessibility that works for the app, such as `kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlockedThisDeviceOnly`, never in `UserDefaults`, property lists or plain files.
Sign users in through `ASWebAuthenticationSession`, with the authorization code flow and PKCE (`AUTH-2`), never in a `WKWebView`.

Keep App Transport Security on: don't set `NSAllowsArbitraryLoads`, fix a server that fails the ATS checks instead of adding an exception, and limit any exception you can't avoid to the domains that need it.

Add a privacy manifest (`PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy`) to the app that declares the data it collects and an approved reason for each required reason API it uses, use the SDKs on Apple's list only in versions that include their privacy manifest (and their signature, if you add them as binaries), and compare the privacy report that Xcode generates from all the manifests with the App Store privacy details before each release.

Save the user's work when the scene phase changes to `.background`, because the app may be terminated soon after, and restore lightweight UI state, such as the selected tab, with `@SceneStorage`. Keep model data and sensitive data out of `@SceneStorage`.

Do background work only through the system's mechanisms: finish a task the user started with `beginBackgroundTask(withName:expirationHandler:)`, transfer large files with a background `URLSession`, and schedule refreshes and maintenance as `BGAppRefreshTask` and `BGProcessingTask` requests.

Persist structured app data with SwiftData, or Core Data, and version the schema from the first release: describe each released schema with a `VersionedSchema`, and the migrations between them with a `SchemaMigrationPlan`.

Make HTTP requests with `URLSession` and its async methods, set `waitsForConnectivity` so that a request waits for a network instead of failing at once, and keep the data the user needs offline in local storage.

Use the built-in text styles, and make any custom font scale the same way, so that text follows Dynamic Type, give every meaningful image and custom control a VoiceOver label, and hide decorative images from VoiceOver.
Write unit tests with Swift Testing and UI tests with XCTest and XCUIAutomation, in a test pyramid (`TEST-1`), and run them on every pull request with `xcodebuild test` or Xcode Cloud.
Sign release builds with cloud-managed certificates, through automatic signing in Xcode or in Xcode Cloud, and never commit exported signing identities or their passwords.
Give every container CPU and memory requests and a memory limit. Set CPU limits only where needed, for example on sensitive workloads.
Configure readiness, liveness and startup probes for their distinct purposes.

Fit graceful shutdown into the Pod's termination grace period: set `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` to cover your slowest shutdown, and use a `preStop` hook if the app needs time before it receives `SIGTERM`.
Run multiple replicas, spread them across nodes and zones, and protect them with PodDisruptionBudgets.
Deploy images by digest, never by a mutable tag such as `:latest`.
Scale stateless workloads horizontally with the HorizontalPodAutoscaler.
Apply the recommended `app.kubernetes.io/*` labels.
Grant least-privilege RBAC, and give each workload its own service account.
Enforce the Restricted Pod Security Standard for application namespaces.
Start each namespace from a default-deny NetworkPolicy and allow only the traffic you need.
Encrypt Secrets at rest, restrict who can read them, and consider an external secret store.
Decide your tenancy model (namespaces, clusters) explicitly.
Let an agent pull the declared state from Git and continuously reconcile the cluster to it (GitOps).
Choose each record's key by the ordering you need: records with the same key go to the same partition, and Kafka keeps order only within a partition.
Choose a topic's partition count when you create it, from the throughput and consumer parallelism you need, with room for growth.
Create topics explicitly with their partition count, replication factor and retention, and turn off automatic topic creation on the brokers.

Set each topic's cleanup policy and retention on purpose: keep records at least as long as consumers may lag behind or need to replay them, and use compaction (`cleanup.policy=compact`) for topics where only the latest value per key matters.
For data you can't afford to lose, use a replication factor of 3, `min.insync.replicas=2` and producer `acks=all`, and leave unclean leader election off.
Keep producer idempotence on, and set `enable.idempotence=true` explicitly, so that conflicting settings fail when the producer is created instead of silently turning it off.
Commit offsets only after the records are processed, and make processing idempotent, because after a failure Kafka redelivers the records since the last commit.
Don't let a record that can't be processed block its partition: after a bounded number of retries, write it with the error details to a dead-letter topic and move on.
Keep the work for each `poll` well within `max.poll.interval.ms`, and lower `max.poll.records` when processing is slow.
For consume-transform-produce flows between Kafka topics, get exactly-once processing from Kafka Streams or a transactional producer, and read the results with `isolation.level=read_committed`.
For queue-style work whose records are independent and need no ordering, consider a share group (production-ready since Kafka 4.2) instead of a consumer group.
Give every topic a schema (Avro, Protobuf or JSON Schema) in a schema registry, and enforce a compatibility type for each subject.
Register schemas from CI after a compatibility check, and set `auto.register.schemas=false` on producers in production.
Authenticate every connection to the brokers with TLS client certificates or SASL over TLS, turn on the `StandardAuthorizer`, and give each application its own principal with only the ACLs it needs.
Run production clusters with dedicated KRaft controller nodes, usually three or five, rather than nodes that are both broker and controller.
Monitor consumer lag for every consumer group, and the brokers' under-replicated and under-min-ISR partition counts, and alert when lag keeps growing or those counts aren't 0.

Never commit the `.env` file: commit `.env.example` with placeholder values, and supply the real values as environment variables on the server or in an encrypted environment file (`php artisan env:encrypt`).
In production, set `APP_DEBUG` to `false` and point the web server's document root at the `public` directory.

Run `php artisan optimize` in every deployment, to cache the configuration, events, routes and views; call `env()` only in the files in `config/`; and restart queue workers and other long-running processes after deploying, for example with `php artisan reload`.

Authorize every action: write the rules for each model in a policy and the other rules in gates, and check them in each controller action, in the Form Request's `authorize()` method, or with the `can` middleware.
Output data with Blade's escaped `{{ }}` syntax, use `{!! !!}` only for HTML you trust, never for content that users supplied, and pass data to JavaScript with `Js::from()`.

Pass values to raw SQL only as bindings, with `?` or named placeholders, in `DB::select()`, `whereRaw()`, `orderByRaw()` and the other raw methods, and never let user input choose column names, including `orderBy` columns.

Validate every request with a Form Request or the validator, pass only the validated data (`$request->validated()` or `safe()`) to `create()`, `fill()` and `update()`, and declare each model's mass-assignable attributes with the `Fillable` attribute (the `$fillable` property before Laravel 13) instead of unguarding the model.
