Validate the type and size of every upload with the `File` rule, for example `File::types([...])->max('10mb')` or `File::image()`, and store it under a generated name with `store()` or `hashName()`, never a name built from `getClientOriginalName()`, `getClientOriginalExtension()` or other user input.

Keep browser routes in the `web` middleware group, where the `PreventRequestForgery` middleware checks them, add `@csrf` to every `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` and `DELETE` form, and exclude only routes that can't send a token, such as third-party webhooks, from CSRF protection.
Change the schema only through migrations in `database/migrations`, run them in each deployment with `php artisan migrate --force`, and add `--isolated` when several servers deploy at once.

Eager load the relationships that each query's results use, with `with()` or `load()`, and call `Model::preventLazyLoading(! $this->app->isProduction())` in `AppServiceProvider`, so that lazy loading, the cause of N+1 queries, throws an exception in development and tests.

Wrap writes that must succeed or fail together in `DB::transaction()`, pass `attempts` to retry on deadlocks, and dispatch queued jobs from inside a transaction only after it commits, with the queue connection's `after_commit` option or `->afterCommit()`.

Run slow work, such as processing uploaded files, in queued jobs; make each job safe to run more than once, keep each worker's `--timeout` several seconds shorter than the connection's `retry_after`, limit the attempts, and keep failed jobs in the `failed_jobs` table to inspect and retry them.

Write most tests as feature tests that send HTTP requests to the application and assert on the response and the database, reset the database for each test with `RefreshDatabase`, and create test data with model factories.
Check the code style with Laravel Pint, and analyse the code with Larastan, the PHPStan extension for Laravel, in CI.
Run a Laravel release that still receives security fixes, on a PHP branch that is still supported, and plan each upgrade before the support ends.
Verify every purchase on your own server before granting it, and keep entitlements and currency balances there, not on the device.
Complete a purchase only after granting it: acknowledge or consume Google Play purchases from your backend, and finish App Store transactions after the content is delivered.

Process the stores' server notifications on your backend, Real-time developer notifications from Google Play and App Store Server Notifications V2, to keep subscriptions current and to claw back refunded or voided purchases.
Show the odds of each item type before a player buys randomised items such as loot boxes.
Treat each store's build requirements as release blockers with deadlines: Google Play's target API level and Play Billing Library version, and the App Store's minimum Xcode and SDK version.

Declare what the game and every SDK in it collect: keep the App Store privacy details and privacy manifests, and Google Play's Data safety form, accurate, and ask for permission through App Tracking Transparency before tracking players on iOS.

Decide the target audience before choosing ad, analytics and social SDKs, and answer both stores' age-rating questionnaires accurately. If children are part of the audience, follow Google Play's Families policies and the App Store's rules for kids' apps.
Run live operations, such as events, offers and balance changes, from remote configuration and downloadable data with safe in-app defaults, not from downloaded code.
Track user-perceived crash and ANR rates for every release, and keep them under Android vitals' bad-behavior thresholds: 1.09% and 0.47% overall, and 8% on any phone model.
Keep the first download small: ship what the first session needs in the base app, and deliver the rest as asset packs with Play Asset Delivery and Background Assets.
Protect ranked play, trading, rewards and other economic features by checking app and device integrity on your server, with the Play Integrity API and App Attest.
Release updates gradually, with staged rollouts on Google Play and phased release on the App Store, and halt or pause the rollout when crash or ANR rates rise.
Cap the frame rate at what the game needs, and lower it and the rendering load when the device heats up, before the system throttles the game.

Design each collection from the application's read and write patterns: embed data that is read or updated together, and reference data that grows without bound, has many items on the child side, is written at different times or exists on its own.
Keep documents bounded: cap arrays with the subset pattern or move their items to a separate collection, and move fields that aren't read together into separate documents.
When the shape of a document changes, add a `schemaVersion` field, and make the code's queries and updates handle every version that can still be in the collection.
Once a collection's schema is established, add a `$jsonSchema` validator and keep the default behavior, which rejects invalid inserts and updates.

Create an index for every frequent query, order compound index keys by the ESR guideline (equality, then sort, then range), and check each query with `explain("executionStats")`: it should use an index scan (`IXSCAN`) and examine about as many documents as it returns.
If you shard a collection, choose a shard key with high cardinality, evenly spread and non-monotonic values, that most queries include, so that they go to one shard.

Write data you can't lose with `w: "majority"`, the default, on replica sets with at least three data-bearing voting members, and read from the primary with `"majority"` read concern where a client must read its own writes.

Use multi-document transactions only where several documents must change atomically, run them with the driver's callback API, which retries transient errors, and keep each one well under the 60-second default limit.

Leave retryable writes on, the driver default, and handle what they don't cover: retry failed operations with exponential backoff where that is safe (`OPS-3`), and make multi-document updates and deletes idempotent.

Create one `MongoClient` per process when it starts, outside request and serverless handlers, and reuse it for every operation; size `maxPoolSize` from the number of concurrent requests, starting at 110–115% of the typical number.

Never expose MongoDB to the internet. Self-managed: bind it to private interfaces, firewall the port so that only application hosts can reach it, and turn on access control, which is off by default. Atlas: never add `0.0.0.0/0` to the IP access list, and connect staging and production projects through private endpoints.

Never pass request data into a query filter or update document as an object: check that each value is a scalar of the expected type, or wrap it in `$eq`, so that a client can't send query operators such as `{"$ne": null}`.

Give each application its own database user with roles scoped to the databases and actions it needs, never a cluster-wide or administrator role, and require TLS on every connection (`SEC-5`, `SEC-13`). On Atlas, authenticate production workloads with Workload Identity Federation, AWS IAM or X.509 certificates; Atlas recommends password (SCRAM) users only for development and test.

Never build `$where`, `$function` or `$accumulator` expressions from user input, and turn server-side JavaScript off when the application doesn't use it: `--noscripting` or `security.javascriptEnabled: false` on self-managed servers, and the Allow Server-Side JavaScript setting on Atlas.

Back up production clusters with point-in-time recovery, keep a copy in a second region, and test restores regularly (`DATA-8`). On Atlas, turn on Cloud Backup with Continuous Cloud Backup, multi-region snapshot distribution and a Backup Compliance Policy.

Choose the upgrade path on purpose. On Atlas clusters that upgrade automatically, declare the Stable API version in a strict client; elsewhere, test each new major version on a staging deployment first, upgrade before the current one reaches end of life, and raise the feature compatibility version only after testing, because after that you can't downgrade.
Treat every Server Action as a public endpoint: authenticate, authorize and validate its input inside the action.
Give an environment variable the `NEXT_PUBLIC_` prefix only if its value may be public.
Put data access in a server-only Data Access Layer that checks authorization and returns minimal data transfer objects (DTOs).
Pass Client Components, and return from Server Actions, only the fields the UI renders.
Add `import 'server-only'` to modules that use secrets or the database.
Keep `"use client"` boundaries small: mark the interactive components, not whole layouts or pages, and pass server-rendered content to them as `children` or props.
Decide caching per data source, and invalidate the cache in every mutation that changes the data.
Read data in Server Components and change it with Server Actions.
Avoid request waterfalls: start independent requests in parallel, and stream slow parts behind `<Suspense>` or `loading.js`.
Return expected errors, such as failed validation, from Server Actions as values, and let `error.js` and `global-error.js` boundaries catch uncaught exceptions.
Use `next/image`, `next/font` and `next/script` instead of plain `` tags, font links and script tags.
Don't block the event loop.
Await or return every promise, and don't pass async functions where the caller ignores the returned promise.
Validate all external input, such as request bodies, query strings and messages, at runtime with a schema library.
Commit the lockfile, install with `npm ci`, and check dependencies for known vulnerabilities in CI.
Run only Active LTS or Maintenance LTS releases of Node.js in production.
Treat unknown errors as fatal: log them, shut down gracefully and let the platform restart the process.
Structure the service by business components, each with its own entry points, domain logic and data access, and keep web-framework objects out of the domain logic.
Type-check Node.js services in CI with `tsc`, and set `module` to `nodenext`.
Shut down gracefully on `SIGTERM`: fail the readiness check, stop accepting connections, finish in-flight requests, close resources, then exit.
Log structured JSON to stdout with a mature logger such as Pino, add request context with child loggers, and redact secrets.
Handle errors in one central handler that every entry point (HTTP routes, jobs, message consumers) calls, and throw only `Error` objects or subclasses of it.
Set HTTP server timeouts and connection limits, and put a reverse proxy in front of the service.
Define SLOs from user-facing SLIs, and use the error budget to balance reliability against release speed.
Monitor the four golden signals for every user-facing service: latency, traffic, errors and saturation.
Put a timeout on every remote call, and retry only with capped exponential backoff and jitter.
Design to prevent cascading failures, for example with load shedding and by avoiding retry storms.
Stop calling a failing dependency with a circuit breaker, and isolate resources with bulkheads.
Avoid fallback paths that are rarely exercised.
Buffer bursts of load with queues between producers and consumers.
Verify resilience with controlled chaos experiments.
Keep config in the environment, treat backing services as attached resources, and run stateless processes.
Expose health endpoints that load balancers and orchestrators can probe.
Instrument with OpenTelemetry and follow its semantic conventions, so telemetry is portable and correlated.
Run blameless postmortems and track their action items.
Run production across at least two independent failure domains, such as availability zones, with enough spare capacity to lose one without scaling up.
Define infrastructure and platform configuration as code in version control, and change it only through a reviewed pipeline, not by hand in a console or dashboard.
Make processes disposable: on `SIGTERM`, stop taking new work, finish or hand back the work in flight, and exit within the platform's grace period.
Write structured logs that carry the trace context, to stdout or through a log appender, and ship them to a central store with the retention you need.
Set `service.name` explicitly in every service, with the same value for all instances of the service, and add `service.version` and `deployment.environment.name` as resource attributes.

Before you name a custom attribute or metric, look for it in the semantic conventions; when none fits, prefix the new name with your company's reverse domain name, such as `com.acme.`, or with your application's name.
Propagate trace context across every process boundary, including queues: keep the default W3C Trace Context propagator for HTTP and gRPC, and have producers attach the context to each message.
Start with zero-code instrumentation or instrumentation libraries for your frameworks and clients, then add code-based spans, attributes and metrics for the business operations that matter.
Correlate logs with traces: keep your logging library, connect it to OpenTelemetry with a log appender (bridge) so that each record carries the active trace and span IDs, and prefer structured logs.
Keep span names and metric attributes low-cardinality: use route templates such as `/users/{id}` instead of raw paths, and keep user IDs, request IDs and other unbounded values off metric attributes.

Treat trace context from outside as untrusted: ignore or sanitize incoming trace headers from callers you don't trust, don't send internal context to external services, and never put credentials or personal data in baggage.

Choose sampling deliberately: don't sample when you produce little data, use consistent probability (head) sampling to cut volume cheaply, and add tail sampling in a Collector tier when you must keep every error or slow trace.

Make `memory_limiter` the first processor in every Collector pipeline, set `GOMEMLIMIT` to about 80% of the Collector's hard memory limit, and batch data after sampling and filtering, preferably with the exporter's `sending_queue` batching.

Secure every Collector: bind receivers to `localhost` or a specific interface instead of `0.0.0.0`, require TLS and authentication on receivers that other hosts send to, keep credentials out of the configuration file, in a secret store or, where nothing else is available, in environment variables, and include only the components you use.
Send telemetry over OTLP to an OpenTelemetry Collector, running as an agent next to the service or as a gateway, rather than from each service straight to a vendor.

Keep secrets and personal data out of telemetry: don't record what you don't need, and remove, hash or truncate what instrumentation captures anyway, for example with the Collector's `redaction`, `attributes`, `transform` or `filter` processors.
Declare integrity rules as constraints in the database: a primary key on every table, `NOT NULL` on most columns, and foreign key, unique and check constraints where the data needs them.
Store points in time as `timestamptz`, not `timestamp`.
Generate keys with identity columns, such as `id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY`, instead of `serial`.
Use `text` for strings, rather than `char(n)` or a `varchar(n)` with an arbitrary limit.

Add indexes for the queries the application actually runs: find the costly ones with `pg_stat_statements`, check their plans with `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on realistic data, and drop indexes that are never used.
Create and drop indexes on tables in use with `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` and `DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY`.
Set a short `lock_timeout` at the start of each migration, and retry the migration when it times out.
Add foreign key and check constraints to existing tables as `NOT VALID`, then run `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` in a separate transaction.
Put a connection pooler such as PgBouncer between the database and large numbers of clients, such as many app instances or serverless functions, instead of raising `max_connections`.
Keep transactions short, set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` to end abandoned ones, and leave autovacuum on.
Test restores regularly, and check that the restored database works and contains the correct data.
Back up production databases with continuous archiving, base backups plus archived WAL, so that you can restore to any point in time, not only to the last dump.
Connect the application as a role that isn't a superuser and doesn't own the tables, and grant it only the privileges it needs; run migrations as a separate owner role.
Use `scram-sha-256` password authentication over TLS, and have clients verify the server with `sslmode=verify-full`.
When tenants share tables, isolate their rows with row security policies, and make sure the application role isn't the table owner or use `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`.
Run a supported major version, apply each minor release soon after it ships, and upgrade to a newer major version before the current one reaches end of life.
Spend architecture effort on the decisions that are hard to change.
Treat internal quality as a speed investment, not a cost.
Reduce irreversibility where you can.
Separate concerns and encapsulate decisions behind interfaces.
Gather together the things that change for the same reasons; separate those that change for different reasons.
Point dependencies at abstractions and make them explicit.
Decompose by design decisions likely to change, not by processing steps.
Keep each piece of knowledge in one place (DRY).
Don't build capabilities for presumed future needs (YAGNI), but do keep the code easy to change.
Prefer the simplest design that passes the tests, reveals intention, has no duplication and has the fewest elements.
Take on technical debt deliberately and prudently, and know when you're doing it.
Expect system structure to mirror communication structure (Conway's law).
Aim for an architecture where teams can test and deploy independently.
Shape teams to get the architecture you want (Inverse Conway Maneuver).
Draw team boundaries to manage cognitive load, using clear team types and interaction modes.
Collect only the personal data that a feature needs for a purpose you have stated, and don't reuse it for a new purpose that isn't compatible with that one.

Keep an inventory of the personal data each system processes: what data, about whom, for which purpose and on which lawful basis, where it is stored, which services and third parties receive it, and how long it is kept.

Pseudonymise personal data that analytics and other secondary uses need to link but not to identify: replace direct identifiers with the output of a keyed one-way function or a random lookup table, and keep the key or table separate, with tighter access (`SEC-2`).
Use made-up test data in development, test and demo environments, not copies of production personal data.
Make the privacy-protective setting the default: run only the processing each purpose strictly needs, and don't make profiles or user content visible to everyone until the user chooses to.
Record each consent with who gave it, when, for which purposes and what they were shown, and make withdrawing it as easy as giving it, in the same interface.

If children are likely to use the service, give them high-privacy defaults: profiling, geolocation and sharing of their data off unless there is a compelling reason, and only the data that the feature they are using needs.
Set a retention period for each kind of personal data, including the copies in logs, backups, analytics and caches, and enforce it automatically: delete or anonymise the data when its period ends.

Design erasure so that one request removes a user's personal data everywhere it is kept: in every service and replica, search indexes, caches, analytics and data warehouses, and at the processors and other recipients you shared it with.
Let users get a copy of their personal data, and download the data they gave you in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format, such as JSON or CSV, preferably through a self-service tool.

Before adding a third-party SDK or service that receives personal data, such as analytics, advertising, crash reporting or customer support, find out what it collects, switch off what you don't need, and add it to the inventory (`PRIV-2`).

Be able to detect a personal data breach and notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware of it, unless it is unlikely to put people at risk: alert on unusual access to personal data (`SEC-4`), keep a runbook that names who assesses and notifies, and require processors to report breaches to you.

Do a data protection impact assessment before building processing that is likely to be high risk, such as large-scale profiling, tracking people's location or behaviour, combining datasets, or offering online services directly to children, and update it as the design changes.

Know in which countries each service and processor stores or accesses personal data, and cover every transfer out of the EEA or the UK with an adequacy decision or appropriate safeguards, such as standard contractual clauses.
Run a Python version that still receives fixes, and upgrade before its end-of-life date.
Commit a lock file that pins every direct and transitive dependency, install exactly what it lists in CI and deployments, and audit it for known vulnerabilities in CI.
Install each application's dependencies into its own virtual environment, not into the Python that the operating system manages, and treat the environment as disposable.
Describe the project in `pyproject.toml`, use the src layout, and keep tests in a separate `tests/` directory.
When the domain has real business logic, keep it in plain Python modules that import neither the web framework nor the ORM, and let views, routers, tasks and commands call it through a service layer.
In FastAPI, split path operations into `APIRouter` modules by area, and provide shared resources such as database sessions, settings and the current user through dependencies (`Depends`).

Validate all external input at runtime where it enters the application, with Pydantic models (as FastAPI does for request bodies) or with Django forms or Django REST framework serializers, and use only the validated data.
Annotate the code with type hints and run a type checker, such as mypy or Pyright, in CI, pinned with the other development dependencies.

In `async` code, don't call blocking I/O or CPU-heavy functions directly: use async libraries, run blocking calls in a thread with `asyncio.to_thread()` (in Django, `sync_to_async()`), and run CPU-heavy work in an executor such as a process pool.
Run concurrent tasks in an `asyncio.TaskGroup`, or keep a reference to every task you start with `asyncio.create_task()` until it finishes.
Write async code only where a service waits on many I/O operations at once, such as long-lived connections or calls fanned out to other services. Otherwise keep it synchronous.
In Django, never enable `DEBUG` in production, load `SECRET_KEY` and other secrets from the environment or a file, and run `manage.py check --deploy` against the production settings.
Load configuration into one typed settings object, such as a `pydantic-settings` `BaseSettings` class, so that missing or malformed values raise a validation error when the settings load.
Never pass untrusted data to `pickle`, `eval()`, `exec()` or `yaml.load()`, or into a shell command with `shell=True`.
Lint and format with Ruff, and run `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` in CI and in a pre-commit hook.
Write quality requirements as concrete, measurable scenarios, not adjectives.
Pick the few (three to five) quality goals that drive the design and make the trade-offs between them explicit.
Protect key characteristics with automated architectural fitness functions that run in the delivery pipeline.
When the architecture is a key business asset, evaluate it with stakeholders against prioritised scenarios early, before committing.
Declare queues whose messages must survive the loss of a node as quorum queues, and make `quorum` the default queue type of the virtual host.
Publish with publisher confirms, and consume with manual acknowledgements, acknowledging each message only after it has been processed.
Make consumers idempotent: the same message can arrive twice, after a redelivery or when a publisher resends a message whose confirm it didn't receive.
Don't let unroutable messages disappear: publish with the `mandatory` flag and handle returned messages, or give the exchange an alternate exchange.

Handle poison messages with the quorum queue delivery limit and a dead-letter exchange: keep the limit on (20 by default since RabbitMQ 4.0), and dead-letter messages that exceed it to a queue that someone monitors.
Give every consumer a bounded prefetch, starting between 100 and 300, and tune it by measurement.
Retry transient failures with the quorum queue's delayed retry (RabbitMQ 4.3 and later) instead of requeueing at once or building dead-letter cycles with TTLs.
Keep connections long-lived, use separate connections for publishing and consuming, and give each thread its own channel.
Keep queues short: run enough consumers to keep up, cap queue length with a policy, and use a stream instead of a queue for large backlogs, replay or large fan-outs.
Configure dead-lettering, TTLs, length limits and delivery limits through policies, not through `x-` arguments hard-coded in applications.
Delete the default `guest` user, disable anonymous logins, and give each application its own user with only the permissions it needs.
Use TLS for client connections with peer verification, and secure inter-node and CLI traffic too.
Monitor with the built-in Prometheus plugin, and alert on queue depth, unacknowledged messages, consumer counts, connection churn and resource alarms.
Stay on a release series that still has community support, and upgrade along the supported rolling upgrade paths, with all stable feature flags enabled first.
Keep components and hooks pure. Side effects belong in event handlers or Effects.
Keep state minimal.
Don't use Effects to transform data or handle user events.
Put state where it's used, and lift it only as far as the closest common parent.
Treat server state (fetched and cached data) separately from UI state, for example with TanStack Query.
Test components with React Testing Library, which renders them into the DOM and queries them the way users find things.
Start new apps with a framework, or with a build tool such as Vite when you have specific constraints.
Try props and composition before reaching for context.
Extract reusable stateful logic into custom hooks.
Organise larger apps by feature, not by file type.
Move non-view logic (domain, data access) out of components as the app grows.
Track Core Web Vitals as the user-facing performance budget.
Keep the authoritative copy of cached data in a durable data store, and keep data only in Redis when you have configured persistence and replication for it on purpose.
Give cache entries a TTL, even a long one, unless write-through keeps them current, and set `maxmemory` with an eviction policy that fits the workload, such as `allkeys-lru` for a pure cache.
Choose the write strategy per data set: cache-aside (load on a miss, invalidate on write) as the default, and write-through where readers must see a change right after the write.

Plan for a cold or unavailable cache: put a timeout on cache calls (`OPS-3`), make sure the data store can take the load of all misses or cap and shed that load, and load-test with the cache disabled.
Protect expensive entries from cache stampedes: add random jitter to TTLs, let only one caller recompute a missing entry (request coalescing), or refresh hot entries before they expire.
Never call `KEYS` from application code, and avoid other O(N) commands on big keys: iterate with `SCAN`, `SSCAN`, `HSCAN` or `ZSCAN`, keep collections and values small, and watch the slow log.
Name keys with one schema, such as `app:object-type:id[:field]`, with a prefix per application or tenant, and hash long natural keys instead of using them as key names.
On Redis Cluster, put keys that one multi-key command, transaction or script uses into the same hash slot with a hash tag, such as `{user:1000}:cart`, and use hash tags only where you need them.
Use Streams with consumer groups, not Pub/Sub, for messages that must not be lost.
Never expose Redis to the internet or other untrusted networks: bind it to private interfaces, firewall the port so that only the application hosts can reach it, and leave protected mode on.
Authenticate every client as a named ACL user with only the commands and key patterns it needs, turn off the passwordless `default` user, and use TLS for every connection that leaves the host.

Choose persistence by what losing the data would cost: none for a cache you can rebuild, RDB snapshots when losing the last minutes of writes is acceptable, and AOF plus RDB for safety close to PostgreSQL's. Copy RDB snapshots off the machine at least daily.
With replication, turn on persistence on the primary and the replicas, or stop a primary without persistence from restarting automatically.
For automatic failover, run Sentinel, with at least three instances on machines that fail independently, or Redis Cluster, and design for lost writes.
Version libraries, SDKs and other packages that others depend on with Semantic Versioning, and declare what their public API is.
Release 1.0.0 as soon as others use the software in production or depend on its API; stay on 0.y.z only while the API is still unstable.
Consider calendar versioning for applications and products that release on a schedule, have a large or shifting scope, or serve users who shouldn't need to know whether a change is breaking.
Never change a published release: its version, tag and artifacts stay as they are, and every fix ships as a new version.
Build releases with an automated, hermetic build, so that building the same commit again gives the same result, and stamp every artifact with the commit and build it came from.
Release from trunk. If you must maintain older versions, cut a release branch from trunk, fix bugs on trunk first and cherry-pick the fixes into the branch, and never merge the branch back.
Automate version bumps, changelogs, tags and publishing with a release tool that reads the commit history or change files, such as Release Please, semantic-release or Changesets.
If releases are derived from commits, write commit messages, or the titles of squash-merged pull requests, in the Conventional Commits format.

Deprecate before you remove: mark the feature deprecated in a minor release, with a warning in the code and docs that says what to use instead and when it goes away, and remove it only in a later major release.
Keep a changelog or release notes written for users: one entry per version with its date, newest first, with changes grouped as Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed and Security.
If a release breaks users by mistake, publish a new version that restores compatibility and mark the bad one as yanked or deprecated, instead of replacing it.
Keep one version of each dependency across the code you build together (the One-Version Rule), whatever the repository layout.
In a monorepo, make each project a package with declared dependencies and a public entry point, and don't import another project's internal files.
Choose between one repository and several on purpose, and record the decision in an ADR: a monorepo suits projects that change together and share code, but needs build tooling that scales with it.
In a monorepo, let CI build and test only the projects a change affects, with a tool that knows the project graph, and cache task results.
Protect the default branch: merge only through pull requests with passing status checks, block force pushes and deletion, and don't let administrators bypass the rules.
Give every part of the repository an owner in a `CODEOWNERS` file, including the file itself, and require review from code owners on the default branch.
Keep changes small and respond to review requests within one business day, so that branches stay short-lived.
When many people merge into one busy branch, use a merge queue, so that each change is tested together with the changes merged ahead of it before it lands.
Start new apps with Expo and Expo Router, and develop in development builds rather than in Expo Go.

Generate the `ios` and `android` directories with Prebuild (Continuous Native Generation): keep native configuration in the app config and config plugins, keep the generated directories out of Git, and don't edit them by hand.
Write the app in TypeScript with `strict` on (`TS-1`), and turn on Expo Router's typed routes, so that the type checker reports links to routes that don't exist.
Treat the JavaScript bundle and the app config as public: never put secrets in `EXPO_PUBLIC_` variables, the app config or the code, and call services that need a secret through your own server.

Store tokens and other secrets with `expo-secure-store`, which uses the iOS Keychain and the Android Keystore, never in AsyncStorage or a persisted state store, and keep them out of crash reports and analytics.

Sign users in through the system browser with `expo-auth-session` or `react-native-app-auth`, using the authorization code flow with PKCE (`AUTH-2`), never in a WebView, and exchange the code on your server when the provider requires a client secret.

Treat every incoming link as untrusted input: validate its route and query parameters before using them (`SEC-10`), never put tokens or personal data in a link, and use universal links and Android App Links for links that must open only your app.
Declare the required reason APIs that the app and its libraries use in `ios.privacyManifests` in the app config, copying the reasons from each library's `PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy`.

Give every build a runtime version that changes whenever its native code changes, preferably with the `fingerprint` policy, test each update on a preview build of the same runtime version through its own channel, and release it to production as a rollout to a small share of users first. Cancel the rollout, or roll back, if the error rate rises.
Use over-the-air updates for bug fixes and other changes that the stores allow without review, and ship new features and changes to the app's purpose in a store build.

Build and submit releases with EAS Build and EAS Submit from CI, and let EAS manage the signing credentials. If you use local credentials, add `credentials.json` and the keystore and certificate files to `.gitignore` (`SEC-2`).
If your EAS plan includes it, sign updates end to end with `expo-updates` code signing, and keep the private key out of source control.
Render long or growing lists with a virtualized list, `FlatList`, `SectionList` or FlashList, not with `.map()` inside a `ScrollView`, and measure performance in release builds.

Turn on the React Compiler after checking the project with `react-compiler-healthcheck`, and in new code rely on it for memoization, with `useMemo` and `useCallback` only where you need precise control.

Stay on a React Native release that still gets fixes, one of the latest three minor versions, by upgrading one Expo SDK at a time: run `npx expo install --fix` and `npx expo-doctor`, and apply native changes with the Upgrade Helper if you don't use Prebuild.

Test components with Jest, the `jest-expo` preset and React Native Testing Library, finding elements as users do (`WEB-14`), and cover the few critical journeys with Maestro end-to-end flows that run in CI, for example on EAS Workflows.
Deny by default, enforce least privilege, and check authorisation server-side on every request.
Keep secrets out of code and repositories.
Threat model early and revisit it as the design changes.
Log security-relevant events, and keep secrets and sensitive personal data out of logs by removing, masking, hashing or encrypting them.
Give each application and service its own identity, with only the permissions it needs, on every system it connects to, and never let it use a shared, default or administrator account.
Ship secure defaults so customers don't have to harden the product themselves.
Don't grant implicit trust based on network location. Authenticate and authorise every access (zero trust).
Protect the software supply chain with build provenance and continuous dependency health checks.
Use STRIDE to enumerate threats per component, data flow and trust boundary.

Validate all input that crosses a trust boundary on the server, against a schema or an allowlist, before using it, and never deserialize untrusted data with a mechanism that can create arbitrary objects or run code.
Treat everything you ship to a client as public, including browser bundles, page payloads, mobile apps and game builds, and never build secrets into it.

Never keep one user's or one request's data in state that a server process shares between requests, such as module-level variables or singletons: scope it to the request, or keep it in a backing service.
Encrypt every network connection with TLS, including internal connections to databases, caches, message brokers and telemetry collectors, and make clients verify the server's certificate.

Authenticate workloads and pipelines with short-lived credentials issued for their identity, such as cloud managed identities or OpenID Connect workload identity federation, instead of long-lived keys or stored secrets.

Pin every dependency, including packages, base images, CI actions and infrastructure modules, to an immutable version, such as a lock file with hashes, an image digest or a commit SHA, install exactly what is pinned, and let a bot propose updates.
Separate production from non-production, and workloads from each other, with their own accounts or projects, credentials and data stores.

Run only releases of runtimes, frameworks, databases and other platform software that still receive security fixes, apply their patch releases promptly, and plan each upgrade before the end-of-life date.
Inject dependencies through constructors, not into fields.
Package by feature: put the main application class in a root package, give each business capability its own subpackage, and once there are several, enforce the boundaries with Spring Modulith.

Keep secrets out of `application.properties`, `application.yaml` and every other file in the repository: mount them as files and import them with `spring.config.import=configtree:`, or load them from a secrets manager, for example with Spring Cloud Vault.

Bind your own settings to `@ConfigurationProperties` classes instead of scattering `@Value` annotations, and annotate them with `@Validated` and Jakarta Bean Validation constraints, so that Spring Boot validates the values when it binds them.

Declare the authorization of every request in each `SecurityFilterChain`: permit the public paths explicitly, require roles or authorities for the rest, and end with `anyRequest().authenticated()` or `anyRequest().denyAll()`.

Expose only the Actuator endpoints you need over HTTP, and secure every exposed endpoint other than `health`, with Spring Security rules built on `EndpointRequest` or by keeping the endpoints behind a firewall.
Keep CSRF protection on for every endpoint that browsers call with cookies or HTTP Basic credentials, and keep `GET`, `HEAD` and `OPTIONS` requests free of side effects.

Use method security (`@EnableMethodSecurity` with `@PreAuthorize` and `@PostAuthorize`) for checks that depend on a method's arguments or return value, such as ownership of a record, and keep a catch-all rule in the `SecurityFilterChain`.
Manage the schema with Flyway or Liquibase migrations, which Spring Boot runs at startup, and leave `spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto` at `none` or set it to `validate`.

Map every association with `fetch = LAZY`, fetch the data each use case needs up front with `join fetch` or an entity graph (`@EntityGraph` in Spring Data JPA), and set `spring.jpa.open-in-view=false`.
Define transaction boundaries with `@Transactional` on the methods of service classes that carry out one use case across several repository calls, and call those methods from other beans.

On Kubernetes, point the liveness and readiness probes at `/actuator/health/liveness` and `/actuator/health/readiness`, keep checks of external systems out of the liveness group, and give the pod a `preStop` sleep and a termination grace period long enough for the sleep and `spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase`.

Instrument through Micrometer Observation, which Spring Boot uses for metrics and traces, export both over OTLP to an OpenTelemetry Collector, and set the service name with `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` or `management.opentelemetry.resource-attributes`.
Run a Spring Boot generation that still has open-source support, and upgrade to the next minor release before its support ends; run it on a Java LTS release that your JDK distribution still updates.

Enable virtual threads with `spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true` only on Java 21 or later, preferably Java 24 or later, and when you do, set `spring.main.keep-alive=true` and limit concurrency with semaphores or connection pools rather than pools of threads.

Test controllers with `@WebMvcTest` and repositories with `@DataJpaTest`, and run at least the repository and integration tests against the database engine you use in production, started by Testcontainers and connected with `@ServiceConnection`.

Use SQLite where the data is on the same machine as the code that queries it and writers can take turns; choose a client/server database, such as PostgreSQL, when the data is on another machine, many processes must write at the same instant, or the data is heading for terabytes.
Never share a database between processes or machines through a network file system, such as NFS or SMB.
Configure every connection in one place as soon as it opens: `PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON`, a busy timeout, and `PRAGMA trusted_schema=OFF`.

Use WAL mode (`PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL`) for databases that are read while they are written, set `PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL` when each connection opens, and never set `synchronous=OFF` for data you need to keep.
Send all writes through one connection or a serial queue, start transactions that will write with `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`, and keep write transactions short.
Pass every value into SQL as a bound parameter, such as `?` or `:name`, never by building SQL strings from input, and pick table and column names from a fixed list in code.

Record the schema version in `PRAGMA user_version`, and when the app opens a database, apply the missing migrations in order, each in a transaction. For changes that `ALTER TABLE` can't make, follow SQLite's 12-step procedure for rebuilding a table and finish with `PRAGMA foreign_key_check`.
Create new tables as `STRICT` tables once every SQLite version that opens the file is 3.37.0 or later.
Group related writes into one explicit transaction instead of letting each statement commit on its own.

Index the columns that frequent queries filter, sort or join on, including the child columns of foreign keys, check plans with `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN`, and run `PRAGMA optimize` as SQLite recommends: before closing short-lived connections, periodically on long-lived ones, and after schema changes.

Copy a live database only with the online backup API, `VACUUM INTO` or `sqlite3_rsync`, never copy the database file while a connection may be writing to it, and never delete, rename or separate it from its `-wal` or `-journal` file.
Check backups and saves with `PRAGMA integrity_check`, or the faster `quick_check`, before you rely on them, and keep the previous good copy until the new one passes.

Treat a database file that someone else could have written, such as a shared save, a mod or a downloaded file, as untrusted input (`SEC-10`): keep `trusted_schema` off, and in security-sensitive apps run `PRAGMA quick_check` before any other statement, reject files that fail, and set `PRAGMA cell_size_check=ON` and `PRAGMA mmap_size=0`.
If the app runs SQL written by users or mods, turn on `SQLITE_DBCONFIG_DEFENSIVE`, lower the limits with `sqlite3_limit()`, and restrict what statements may do with an authorizer callback.

Upload builds from CI with `steamcmd` under a dedicated Steam build account that has only the *Edit App Metadata* and *Publish App Changes To Steam* permissions, and keep its login token in the CI secret store.
Let CI set builds live only on a beta branch with a password, test each build there, and set it live on the default branch by hand in Steamworks. To roll back, set the previous build live again.

Ship updates and extra content through SteamPipe depots or DLC, not as downloads inside the game, and lay out pack files so that patches stay small: no more than about one or two GB each, grouped by level or feature, with new content in new pack files, no reordered assets or build timestamps, and compression only per asset.

Keep the publisher Web API key and the Encrypted App Ticket key on your servers only, never in the game or its repository, and limit each publisher key to the permissions and calling IP addresses it needs.

Identify players on your game servers and backends by verifying a Steam session ticket, not by a Steam ID that the client reports: a game server or peer passes the ticket to `BeginAuthSession`, and a backend sends a ticket from `GetAuthTicketForWebApi` to the `ISteamUserAuth/AuthenticateUserTicket` Web API.

Run in-game purchases from your server: start each one with `ISteamMicroTxn/InitTxn`, grant the items only after your server's `FinalizeTxn` call succeeds, and call `GetReport` at least once a day to take back the items of refunded and charged-back orders.

Grant Steamworks permissions through groups that contain only the apps each person works on, give each person only the permissions they need, keep *Administrator*, *Manage Users*, *Manage Signing* and *Actual Authority* to a few people, and review who has them regularly.

Let only servers you host set the stats, achievements and leaderboard scores that competition or rewards depend on: set the stat's *Set By* to *Official GS* and register your servers' IP ranges, and set competitive leaderboards' *Writes* to *Trusted*, so that only your server can submit scores, with the `SetLeaderboardScore` Web API.

Write Steam Cloud saves to a folder for each Steam user, such as `{64BitSteamID}` in an Auto-Cloud path, keep Auto-Cloud root paths *Cross-Platform*, split saves into small files by how often they change, and never sync machine-specific settings such as resolution or graphics quality.
Let Steam keep stats and achievements: call `SetStat` whenever a stat changes and `StoreStats` at checkpoints and right after unlocking achievements, and don't keep a copy of them in your own files.

Make the whole game playable with a controller in its default configuration: read input as actions grouped into action sets, through the Steam Input API or your engine's action-based input (`UNREAL-29`, `GODOT-22`), show glyphs for the device in use, accept mouse and controller input at the same time, and open the on-screen keyboard with `ShowGamepadTextInput` or `ShowFloatingGamepadTextInput` when the game needs text.

Save graphics settings for each device and keep them out of Steam Cloud, choose defaults for the detected hardware without hiding any setting, support aspect ratios other than 16:9 and 16:10, and match the display's resolution on first launch.
Make all single-player content playable without an Internet connection, and test it offline, including the first launch on a new Steam account.
Build everything the player needs into the game instead of a separate launcher, choose middleware that runs under Proton, and test the Windows build under Proton, on Linux or a Steam Deck.
Collect crash reports from players' release builds through your engine's crash reporter or a crash-reporting service, and archive the debug symbols of every build you upload, outside the depots.

Sign the Windows executables, libraries and installers you ship, in the release pipeline, with one consistent signing identity, such as Azure Artifact Signing or an OV certificate, and sign after every step that changes the files, such as the Steam DRM wrapper.
Start with a well-structured monolith and split it once the boundaries are understood.
Have rapid provisioning, basic monitoring and rapid deployment in place before adopting microservices.
Organise services around business capabilities and let each service own its data.
Treat microservices as a premium you pay to manage complexity.
Consider a modular monolith: one deployable with strictly enforced module boundaries.
Keep the domain independent of UI, frameworks and databases, so that dependencies point inwards.
Layer presentation, domain and data, but in larger systems make domain modules the top-level split.
Apply CQRS only to the specific parts of a system that need it.
Use event sourcing where a full history of changes is a requirement, not as a default persistence model.
Say which event-driven pattern you mean: event notification, event-carried state transfer, event sourcing or CQRS.
Replace legacy systems incrementally behind a facade (Strangler Fig) rather than with a big-bang rewrite.
Put an anti-corruption layer between your model and legacy or external models.
When extracting services, start with a simple, loosely coupled capability and decouple by business capability, not by technical layer.
Enable Row Level Security on every table in an exposed schema, such as `public`, and grant the `anon` and `authenticated` roles only the operations your app needs.
Never create `security definer` functions in an exposed schema, set `search_path = ''` on every one, and create views with `security_invoker = true` or keep them out of exposed schemas.

Write a separate policy for each operation, name its role with `to authenticated` or `to anon`, compare owner columns with `(select auth.uid())`, add `with check` to insert and update policies, and base authorisation on `app_metadata`, never on `user_metadata`, which users can change themselves.

Test the policies of every table with pgTAP: a test file per table under `supabase/tests` that asserts which operations each role may and may not perform, run with `supabase test db` on every pull request.
Index every column that policies filter on, and wrap `auth.uid()` and `auth.jwt()` in a `select` so that Postgres evaluates them once per statement instead of once per row.
If you enable anonymous sign-ins, check the `is_anonymous` claim in restrictive policies on data that only permanent users may reach, and protect the sign-in endpoint with CAPTCHA.

Keep Storage buckets private unless every file in them may be public, control access with policies on `storage.objects`, for example per user folder, and give temporary access to private files with signed URLs.
Put only the publishable key, or the legacy `anon` key, in clients, and keep secret keys and the `service_role` key in servers and Edge Functions, out of source control.

Check every caller of an Edge Function: keep `verify_jwt` on for functions that users call, and query with the client that applies their RLS policies; use the admin client, which bypasses RLS, only for work that must cross policies, and verify the signature of external webhooks.

Make every schema change, including RLS policies, grants and functions, a migration file in `supabase/migrations` under version control, and never change the production database directly in the dashboard.

Plan backups for your recovery point objective: Supabase backs up only paid-plan projects daily, so on the Free plan export the database regularly with `supabase db dump` and keep the copies off-site, and on paid plans enable point-in-time recovery when losing up to a day of data is too much.

Connect each runtime the way Supabase recommends: clients through the Data API, serverless and edge functions through the shared pooler in transaction mode, with prepared statements off and a pool of one connection per instance, and migrations, `pg_dump` and long-running backends through a direct connection or the pooler's session mode.
Turn on SSL enforcement and network restrictions for the database.
Leave the Spend Cap on, or watch the organization's usage page when it's off, so that an attack or a bug can't run up unlimited charges.

Configure Supabase Auth for production: turn on email confirmations, send auth email through your own SMTP server, enable CAPTCHA on sign-up, sign-in and password reset, let one-time passwords expire within an hour, and review the rate limits.
Write new components in runes mode, and don't use legacy features that have modern replacements, such as `$:` statements, `export let`, `on:` directives, slots, and stores for shared state.
Compute values from state and props with `$derived`, not by assigning state in an `$effect`, and keep `$effect` as an escape hatch for things such as analytics and direct DOM manipulation.
Type-check `.svelte` files in CI with `sv check` (svelte-check).

Share reactive state between components with `$state` objects or classes with `$state` fields, defined in `.svelte.js` or `.svelte.ts` modules, and keep stores for complex asynchronous streams or for when you need manual control over updates.

Never keep user or request data in module-level variables or other shared state on the server: return it from `load`, pass it down as props or through context, and persist it in a database. Keep `load` functions free of side effects for the same reason.

Load data that needs the database, the filesystem or private credentials in server `load` functions (`+page.server.js`), and use universal `load` functions (`+page.js`) only for public APIs or for values that can't be serialized.
Avoid request waterfalls: make dependent backend calls in server `load` functions, use the `fetch` that `load` receives, and call `await parent()` only after the requests that don't depend on it.
Implement mutations as form actions that work without JavaScript, return validation errors with `fail()`, and progressively enhance the form with `use:enhance`.
Choose rendering per route with page options: prerender pages that every user sees the same, server-render dynamic pages, and turn off `ssr` only for pages that can't run on the server.
Replace `adapter-auto` with the adapter for your platform once you've chosen where to deploy, and host the app in the same data center as its backend.
Treat every form action, `+server.js` handler and remote function as a public HTTP endpoint: make sure an authorization check covers it, and validate its input on the server.
Declare environment variables in `src/env.ts`, mark one `public: true` only if its value may be public, and import secrets only from `$app/env/private`.
Check authentication in the `handle` hook or in each `+page.server.js` `load` function, not only in a `+layout.server.js` `load` function.
Put code that uses secrets, the database or other server-only APIs in server-only modules: files with a `server` segment in their name, such as `db.server.ts`, or files in a `server` directory.
Give every page a unique, descriptive `<title>` in `<svelte:head>`, and set the `lang` attribute in `src/app.html`.
Fix the compiler's accessibility warnings, and silence one with `<!-- svelte-ignore -->` only for a false positive, with a note saying why.
Write many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests and very few end-to-end tests.
Keep the software deployable at all times, and prioritise that over new features.
Integrate small changes into the main branch at least daily.
Enforce architecture rules such as layering and dependency direction with automated tests.
Test service boundaries with contract tests rather than relying on slow, brittle end-to-end integration suites.
Decouple deployment from release with feature toggles, and remove toggles once they've served their purpose.
Measure software delivery throughput and instability with the DORA metrics, and use them to improve, not to compare teams.
Store state in a remote backend with locking and encryption at rest, restrict who can read it, and never commit state files.
Give Terraform short-lived credentials, such as OIDC from the CI platform or HCP Terraform dynamic provider credentials, instead of static keys. Never put credentials in provider blocks or variables.
Keep secrets out of state where the provider allows it, with ephemeral values and write-only arguments (Terraform 1.10 and 1.11 or later), and protect saved plan files like state.
Split infrastructure into separate root modules, each with its own state, by environment, blast radius, rate of change and team ownership.
Give each environment its own directory, with its own backend, that calls shared modules. Don't use CLI workspaces for environments that need separate credentials or access controls.
Rename and move resources with `moved` blocks, and keep old `moved` blocks in shared modules.
Keep the module tree flat: compose child modules in the root module and pass their dependencies in as variables.
Write modules that do one thing well at a higher level of abstraction, not thin wrappers around a single resource.
Protect costly stateful resources, such as databases and storage, with `prevent_destroy`, sparingly.
Pin versions: set `required_version`, constrain providers with `~>` in root modules but only by minimum in reusable modules, pin module versions, and commit `.terraform.lock.hcl`.
Run Terraform from a pipeline: plan every change, save the plan with `-out`, and apply exactly that plan after review.
Run `terraform fmt -check`, `terraform validate` and TFLint on every change, and test reusable modules with `terraform test`.
Check plans against security and organisation policies as code before applying them.
Detect drift on a schedule, for example with `terraform plan -detailed-exitcode` or HCP Terraform health assessments.
Keep `strict` on in every project, and don't turn off the checks it includes.
When another tool compiles your TypeScript, turn on `isolatedModules`, add `erasableSyntaxOnly` if that tool only strips types, and type-check with `tsc --noEmit` in CI.
In new projects, also turn on `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` and `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`.
Remove the options that TypeScript 6.0 deprecated, such as `baseUrl`, `moduleResolution: node10`, `target: es5` and AMD or UMD output, instead of silencing the warnings with `ignoreDeprecations`.
Set `module` for the host that loads your code: `nodenext` when Node.js runs it, and `esnext` or `preserve` with `moduleResolution: bundler` when a bundler does.
Turn on `verbatimModuleSyntax`, and import and export types with `import type` and `export type`.
Don't use `any`. Use `unknown` for values whose type you don't know, and narrow them with type guards before you use them.

Type data from outside the program, such as `JSON.parse` results, `fetch` responses, storage and messages, as `unknown`, and check it at runtime before you narrow it to your own types. Don't claim its shape with an `as` assertion.
Model a value that can be in one of several states as a discriminated union, and make `switch` statements over it exhaustive with a `never` check.
Check a library with the settings its consumers might use: `module` set to `node18` or `nodenext` rather than `moduleResolution: bundler`, `declaration` on, and the lowest `target` you support.

Publish declaration files with the package and point to them from `exports`: put the `types` condition first in each entry, and give the ES module and CommonJS entry points separate declaration files.
Give each environment, such as browser, server, worker and tests, its own `tsconfig.json`, and connect them, and the packages of a monorepo, with project references built by `tsc --build`.
Turn on `isolatedDeclarations` only when declaration emit limits your build, as in large monorepos, or when another tool generates your declaration files.
Keep logic that doesn't need the engine in plain C# classes, with MonoBehaviours as thin adapters.
Separate UI from game logic with Model-View-Presenter (or MVC).
Model complex behaviour, such as characters, AI and game flow, with the State pattern instead of growing `switch` statements.
Wrap player and AI actions in commands when you need undo, replay, rebinding or queuing.
Put designer-tunable, shared data in ScriptableObject assets, not hard-coded values or copies on every prefab.
Don't use ScriptableObjects as save-game storage.
Use ScriptableObject-based enums when designers need to add values without code changes.
Make dependencies explicit through serialized references, constructor or method injection, or a DI container (for example VContainer), rather than singletons and scene-wide `Find` lookups everywhere.
Don't rely on the order in which Unity calls the same event function (`Awake`, `Start`, …) on different objects.
Decouple systems with events.
For asynchronous code, use `Awaitable` with async/await (Unity 2023.1+) or coroutines, and know which thread each continuation runs on.
For multiplayer, choose the netcode stack with the Multiplayer Center and study Boss Room before designing your own architecture.
Choose the UI system (UI Toolkit or uGUI) per use case using Unity's comparison.
Choose the Entities package (DOTS/ECS) deliberately for large simulations.
Start new projects on the Universal Render Pipeline (URP), and choose HDRP only for a PC or console project that needs its high-end features. Don't start a new title on the Built-in Render Pipeline.

In URP and HDRP, follow Unity's draw-call recommendations: enable the SRP Batcher and the GPU Resident Drawer, turn off static batching and the materials' *Enable GPU Instancing* checkbox, share materials, and use Material Variants rather than `MaterialPropertyBlock` for objects that differ only in property values.
Write custom shaders in Shader Graph by default, bring in hand-written HLSL through Custom Function nodes, and keep any fully hand-written URP or HDRP shader compatible with the SRP Batcher.

Declare keywords that only materials set with `shader_feature_local` (in Shader Graph, keep the keyword's default *Shader Feature* definition), keep `multi_compile` for branches that C# switches at run time, and use `dynamic_branch` for simple, balanced branches on fast GPUs.

Strip the shader variants the build doesn't need, and check the count after every build: turn on *Strip Unused Variants* and *Strip Unused Post Processing Variants* in the URP Graphics settings, turn off unused features in every URP asset the build includes, remove keywords in *Shader Build Settings* (Unity 6.3 LTS and later), and strip the rest with `IPreprocessShaders`.

On DirectX 12, Vulkan and Metal, record the pipeline state objects (PSOs) the game uses into a `GraphicsStateCollection` from a development build, one collection per graphics API and platform, ship the collections, and warm them up during loading screens with `WarmUp` or `WarmUpProgressively`.

Set texture import settings for each platform in the platform overrides: ASTC on mobile, XR and the web, BC7, DXT or BC6H on desktop, the lowest *Max Size* that looks acceptable, and *Read/Write* off. Apply them through presets, so that new imports get them automatically.

Give meshes that are seen at varying distances levels of detail: generate Mesh LODs on import (Unity 6.2 and later) to cut triangles at little memory cost, and use LOD Groups where a lower level must also cut materials or draw calls, or needs explicit transition sizes.
Inspect batching in the Frame Debugger and GPU cost in the Rendering Debugger, both of which can also inspect a built player.
Profile with the Unity Profiler connected to a build running on the target device, early and before and after every optimisation, not only in the Editor.
Pair every Addressables load with a release.
Avoid managed allocations in per-frame code paths to prevent garbage-collector spikes.
Keep the `Resources` folder for prototypes and small bootstrap data. Load game content through Addressables (or AssetBundles).
Pool objects that are created and destroyed often, such as projectiles, effects and UI list items, using `UnityEngine.Pool`.

Localize with the Unity Localization package: keep text in String Tables, make entries that insert values or counts Smart Strings, which take named placeholders and choose plural forms by the CLDR rules, and swap language-specific textures, audio and other assets through Asset Tables.
Agree on one folder structure and naming convention, write it down, and keep your own assets separate from third-party assets.
Know Unity's reserved folder names (`Editor`, `Resources`, `StreamingAssets`, `Plugins`, …) and use them only for their purpose.
Agree on a team C# style guide, starting from Unity's example and adapting it. Apply it consistently, and enforce formatting with an EditorConfig file.
Split code into assemblies with Assembly Definition files once the project grows.

Mirror the architecture in assemblies, for example `Game.Core` (no engine-specific dependencies where practical), `Game.Gameplay`, `Game.UI`, `Game.Editor` and `*.Tests`, so that wrong-way references fail to compile.
Move systems that several projects share into custom UPM packages that follow the standard package layout.
Keep `.meta` files visible and committed, and keep asset serialization on Force Text, so that assets diff and merge.
Start from the community Unity `.gitignore` so that generated folders such as `Library/` and `Temp/` are never committed.
Configure UnityYAMLMerge (Smart Merge) as the merge tool for scenes and prefabs.
Enter Play mode without domain reload for faster iteration.
Inject dependencies into the plain C# classes that hold the logic, so that Edit Mode tests can substitute fakes.
Run the tests from the command line in batch mode as part of the build, so CI runs them on every change.
Write plain NUnit `[Test]` tests in Edit Mode for logic that doesn't need Play mode, and use `[UnityTest]` Play Mode tests for runtime behaviour that spans frames or needs a scene.
Put tests in their own test assemblies that reference the assemblies under test.
Hold UObject references that must keep their target alive in `UPROPERTY` members, preferably `TObjectPtr`, and use `TWeakObjectPtr` for references that must not.

Put match rules in the game mode, which exists only on the server, state that all players need in the game state, per-player state in the player state, and anything that must survive a level change in the game instance or its subsystems.
Write core systems, high-frequency logic and data-heavy work in C++ base classes, and expose a small API that designers extend in Blueprint subclasses.

Put game-wide services in subsystems (`UGameInstanceSubsystem`, `ULocalPlayerSubsystem`, `UEngineSubsystem` or `UEditorSubsystem`) instead of adding them to a custom game instance or overriding engine classes.
Split code into modules with explicit dependencies in their `Build.cs` files: keep editor-only code in `Editor` modules, and prefer private dependencies to public ones.
Use the Gameplay Ability System for games built around many abilities, attributes and status effects, especially multiplayer ones.
Build optional or frequently changing features as Game Feature plugins, so that unrelated features can't depend on each other by accident.
Keep the server authoritative: clients request actions through Server RPCs, and the server validates them before it changes any state.
Prefer replicated properties with RepNotify to RPCs, use multicast RPCs sparingly, and make frequently called RPCs unreliable.
Reference assets that aren't always needed with soft references (`TSoftObjectPtr`, `TSoftClassPtr`), and load them asynchronously.
Profile early and often on the target hardware, with Unreal Insights.
Register the content you load on demand, such as levels and data assets, as primary assets with the Asset Manager, and use asset bundles to control which secondary assets load with them.
Turn content rules, such as naming conventions and size or performance budgets, into Data Validation rules, and run the `DataValidation` commandlet in CI.
Write automated tests with the Automation Test Framework, use Low-Level Tests for pure unit tests, and run both from the command line in CI.
Keep One File Per Actor on (the default with World Partition), so that several people can change actors in the same level at once.

Keep all user-facing text in `FText`, created from text properties in assets, `LOCTEXT` macros in C++ or String Tables, and build messages with `FText::Format` and its `plural`, `ordinal` and `gender` argument modifiers.
Keep PSO precaching on, hold the first loading screen until `FShaderPipelineCache::NumPrecompilesRemaining()` reaches zero, and test first-run smoothness with `-clearPSODriverCache`.

Give the team a shared Derived Data Cache, so that each shader and other derived asset is built once for everyone: a Zen Storage Server or a network drive for people in one office, and Unreal Cloud DDC for a distributed team.
Build materials as a few parameterized parent materials, create the variations as Material Instances, and use Material Instance Dynamic only for values that change at run time.

Keep material permutations down: use few static switch parameters and few combinations of them across instances, and keep usage flags to the kinds of mesh a material is really used on, because each combination and each flag compiles more shaders.
Decide for each target platform, before content production starts, whether to use Nanite and Lumen.

Set rendering quality for each platform and device in `Config/DefaultDeviceProfiles.ini`, through the scalability groups (`sg.*`) and console variables, and test every quality level on low-, mid- and high-spec hardware.

Don't poll for changes on Tick: run occasional logic from events, delegates or timers, give logic that must repeat but not every frame a tick interval, and turn ticking off on Actors and components that don't need it.
Represent statuses, object types and gameplay events as hierarchical Gameplay Tags of the form `Movement.Mode.Swimming`, registered in `.ini` tag lists or as native tags in C++.
Model AI and other state-driven logic, such as game flow, in StateTree, Epic's general-purpose hierarchical state machine, or, for AI, in Behavior Trees with a Blackboard.

Put designer-tunable data in Data Tables, whose rows are C++ structs and which designers can import from CSV or JSON files, or in Data Assets, and make content that the Asset Manager loads on demand a Primary Data Asset.
Save games through your own `USaveGame` subclasses, with separate classes for globally unlocked features and for each playthrough's data, and save with `AsyncSaveGameToSlot` during play.

Choose how Blueprints communicate by the relationship between them: a direct reference for one Actor talking to one specific other, an event dispatcher to tell any number of listeners that something happened, and a Blueprint Interface to call the same function on unrelated classes that each respond in their own way.

Handle player input with Enhanced Input: an Input Action for each thing the player can do, Input Mapping Contexts that you add, remove and prioritize as the player's situation changes, and Player Mappable Input Configs for control presets.

Keep game logic out of UMG widgets: give widgets their data through viewmodels and View Bindings (the UMG Viewmodel plugin, in Beta), which update a widget only when a value changes, and set the *Property Binding Rule* to *Prevent* so that nobody adds legacy property bindings.
In games with many players and many replicated Actors, decide what each client receives with the Replication Graph, and evaluate Iris, which is still Experimental, before relying on it.

Keep garbage-collection hitches out of gameplay: pool Actors that are spawned and destroyed often when the CPU budget is tight, and collect garbage manually where a spike is tolerable, such as behind a loading screen.
Find out what an asset pulls into memory with the Reference Viewer and its Size Map, and track memory at run time on each target platform with the Low-Level Memory Tracker and Memory Insights.

Build large open worlds with World Partition, which stores the world in one level divided into grid cells and streams the cells by distance, instead of dividing the map into sublevels and streaming them by hand.

Agree on an asset naming convention early in development, starting from Epic's `[AssetTypePrefix]_[AssetName]_[Descriptor]_[OptionalVariantLetterOrNumber]` scheme, and keep each person's experiments in their own Developers folder, which no asset outside it may reference.
After moving or renaming assets, fix up the redirectors they leave behind, in the Content Browser or with the `ResavePackages` commandlet and `-fixupredirects`, and submit the resaved packages.

Keep generated folders out of version control: start from the community `UnrealEngine.gitignore`, which ignores `Binaries/`, `Intermediate/`, `Saved/` and `DerivedDataCache/`, or, with Perforce, from Epic's example `.p4ignore`.
Connect the editor to revision control, and turn on its automatic checkout or checkout prompt on modification, so that assets are checked out, and with that locked, before anyone changes them.

Script CI builds, cooks and tests with BuildGraph, and give artists and designers the editor binaries that CI builds, for example through Unreal Game Sync with Perforce, so that they don't have to compile.

Iterate on C++ with Live Coding, which is on by default and is significantly faster and more flexible than Hot Reload, and keep Object Reinstancing on so that structural changes reach existing objects.

Write tests for code that needs engine systems as Automation Spec or CQTest tests rather than with the plain automation test macros, and test gameplay that spans frames or needs a level with Functional Tests, Actors placed in a test level.

Follow Epic's test design guidelines: don't assume the state of the game or the editor, because tests can run in any order or in parallel on several machines, leave files on disk as you found them, and mark a test as a Smoke test only if it finishes within a second.
Run boot tests and automation tests on packaged builds for each target platform with Gauntlet, not only in the editor.

Catch rendering regressions with screenshot comparison tests: place Functional Screenshot Test Actors in test levels, turn off noisy rendering features, set a tolerance, and review differences in the Screenshot Comparison browser.
Never mutate props, including nested properties of object props: emit an event so that the parent changes its own state, or use `defineModel()` for two-way binding.
Write application components as Single-File Components with the Composition API and `<script setup>`.
Derive values with `computed`, keep computed getters free of side effects, and use watchers only for side effects in reaction to state changes.
Declare props and emitted events with types, such as `defineProps<Props>()`, and type-check `.vue` files in CI with `vue-tsc`.

Extract reusable stateful logic into composables: name them `useX`, accept refs or getters and read them with `toValue()`, return a plain object of refs, and call them synchronously in `<script setup>` or `setup()`.

In server-rendered apps, never keep user or request data in module-level state: create the app, router and stores for each request, and in Nuxt keep shared state in `useState` or Pinia, not in refs exported from a module.
Use Pinia for state that many components share, instead of hand-rolled global `reactive()` objects.
In Nuxt, load the data a page renders with `useFetch` or `useAsyncData`, keep `$fetch` for requests that user events trigger, and use `pick` or `transform` to keep only the fields the page renders.

Render the same output on the server and in the browser: use SSR-safe composables, keep browser-only code in `onMounted()` or `<ClientOnly>`, and don't render values that differ between the two, such as the current time.

Use server-side rendering or static generation, for example with Nuxt, when page load performance or SEO matters, and a client-side SPA only when they don't. In Nuxt, set the rendering mode per route with `routeRules`.
Lazy-load route components with dynamic imports.
After each route change, move focus back to the start of the page, just before a skip link to the main content.
Never use untrusted content as a Vue template, and never mount Vue on server-rendered HTML that contains user-provided content.
Give an environment variable the `VITE_` prefix, or put a value in Nuxt's `runtimeConfig.public`, only if it may be public.
Run unit and component tests with Vitest, give each component its own component test, and in those tests interact with the component as a user would instead of mocking its child components.
Target WCAG 2.2 Level AA as the minimum for every page and component.
Use native HTML elements, such as `button`, `a`, `input` and `select`, before ARIA.
Run automated accessibility checks in CI, and also test by hand with a keyboard and a screen reader.
Measure Core Web Vitals from real users at the 75th percentile, separately for mobile and desktop, and set priorities from that field data.
Ship less JavaScript: split off code that the first render doesn't need, remove unused code, and use Baseline platform features instead of JavaScript reimplementations.
Give every image and embed explicit dimensions, offer sizes that fit the layout with `srcset` and `sizes`, and lazy-load only images outside the initial viewport.

Put a content hash or version in the URLs of static assets and cache them for a long time with `immutable`, and serve HTML with `Cache-Control: no-cache` (plus `private` when it's personalised) so that it's always revalidated.

Render untrusted data through the framework's automatic escaping or `textContent`, and sanitize it with DOMPurify before it reaches an HTML sink such as `innerHTML` or React's `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`.
Send security headers with every response: `Strict-Transport-Security`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, a `Referrer-Policy`, and the CSP `frame-ancestors` directive against framing.
Add a strict, nonce- or hash-based Content Security Policy as a second layer of defence against XSS, and try it in `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` mode before enforcing it.
Load third-party scripts with Subresource Integrity, or serve your own reviewed copies.
Choose a Baseline target, such as Baseline Widely available, from your users' browser data, and set it once in Browserslist so that build and lint tools share it.
Build core user journeys with progressive enhancement: HTML that works on its own first, then CSS and JavaScript that enhance it, so that a script that fails to load doesn't stop users.
Find elements in tests the way users find them: by role and accessible name first, then by label or text, and by test ID only when nothing visible identifies the element.

Never wait for a fixed time in a test: use actions that wait automatically and assertions that retry until the page reaches the expected state, such as Playwright's `await expect(locator).toBeVisible()` or Testing Library's `findBy` queries.

Isolate every test: run it in a fresh browser context, let it build the state and data it needs instead of relying on earlier tests, and when tests change server-side state, give each parallel worker its own user account.
Run the end-to-end tests in CI on every pull request, in each browser engine you support, and keep a trace of every failure.
Treat a flaky test as a bug: quarantine it outside the blocking pipeline, file a bug for it, and fix it within a set time.
Test components in a real browser, for example with Vitest Browser Mode, and keep end-to-end tests to the few user journeys that carry the product's core value.
Mock HTTP at the network level, for example with Mock Service Worker, instead of mocking `fetch` or your API client modules, and make requests without a handler fail the test.

Keep visual comparison (screenshot) tests to a few stable pages and components, hide dynamic content such as dates, and create and compare the screenshots in the same environment, with the same operating system and browser versions.
Before you choose a scripting language, renderer or plugins, check what the engine's web export supports.
Serve the engine's precompressed build files over HTTPS with the matching `Content-Encoding` header, `gzip` for `.gz` and `br` for `.br` files, and serve `.wasm` files as `application/wasm`.
Export without threads unless you control the headers of every page that hosts the game.

Ship GPU texture formats for both desktop and mobile browsers: in Unity, make two builds, one with DXT for desktop and one with ASTC for mobile browsers, and in Godot, turn on VRAM texture compression for both desktop and mobile in the web export preset.
Set a download budget for the first load and for the whole game, from the portals and devices you target, and check every build against it.
Download only what the first scene needs before play starts, load the rest per scene in the background, and let the engine cache downloaded files on the player's device.
When the page becomes hidden, pause the game, suspend the `AudioContext` and save progress.

If you write your own game loop, drive it with `requestAnimationFrame`, request the next frame before doing the frame's work, and advance the fixed time step of `GAMEDEV-1` from the callback's timestamp.
Start audio from the player's first click, tap or key press, for example on a "tap to play" screen, and resume the `AudioContext` from a later tap whenever it is suspended or interrupted.

Handle mouse, touch and pen with Pointer Events on the game canvas, set `touch-action: none` on the canvas only, and if the game runs in mobile browsers, give it touch controls and a layout for each orientation it supports.

Read gamepads by polling `navigator.getGamepads()` once per frame, ask the player to press a button before expecting a controller to appear, and let players remap buttons when a gamepad's `mapping` isn't `"standard"`.
Request fullscreen and pointer lock only from a click or key-press handler, handle a refusal, and check that the page embedding the game allows them.

Store saves in IndexedDB rather than `localStorage`, request persistent storage when the player first saves, and keep a copy of progress that matters on a server, such as a portal's cloud save or your own backend.

If you publish on web game portals, integrate each portal's SDK and meet its technical requirements from the start: report loading and gameplay events, show ads only through the portal's SDK, and bundle every asset into the build.

Free GPU resources explicitly when a level or scene ends: in three.js, call `dispose()` on geometries, materials, textures and render targets, and in Phaser, remove assets that only the finished scene used.
Profile web builds in the browser on the slowest device you support, and move heavy work that doesn't draw, such as pathfinding or procedural generation, to Web Workers.
